stem: A patient underwent a dental procedure and subsequently develops jaundice and chills. Ultrasound reveals a 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver
why_right: A "dental procedure" followed by "jaundice and chills" and a "6-cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver" points to a pyogenic liver abscess from bacteremic seeding. An abscess of this size will not resolve on antibiotics alone, so the appropriate initial management is image guided percutaneous drainage combined with IV broad spectrum antibiotics, which also gives pus for culture.
why_wrong_block: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for a septic patient with a large pyogenic abscess; therapy starts IV and is combined with drainage. Antibiotics alone suit small abscesses (roughly under 3 cm) or an amoebic abscess treated with metronidazole.
key_concept:
Liver abscess: decide pyogenic vs amoebic, then size.
  • Pyogenic: biliary disease, bacteremia (dental, GI source); chills, high fever
  • Pyogenic, larger abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics
  • Pyogenic, small abscess: IV antibiotics (aspiration if needed)
  • Amoebic (travel, Entamoeba serology): metronidazole first, even if large
  • Open surgery: rupture, failed percutaneous drainage, multiloculated thick pus
  • Hydatid: albendazole, avoid blind aspiration
exam_pearl: Amoebic abscess = metronidazole first regardless of size; pyogenic large abscess = drain.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0163).

stem: A patient sustained a high-velocity trauma and is hypotensive despite receiving IV fluids. Xray shows an openbook pelvic fracture. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A high-velocity injury with an open-book pelvic fracture and hypotension despite IV fluids means ongoing pelvic bleeding from the widened pelvic ring. The immediate step in the primary survey (circulation) is a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters: it closes the ring, reduces pelvic volume and tamponades venous and bony bleeding, while blood transfusion is started.
why_wrong_block:
B. External fixation stabilizes the pelvis more definitively but takes time and theatre resources; it follows the binder in an unstable patient, not before it.
C. Surgery (laparotomy or pre-peritoneal packing) is for persistent instability after the binder and transfusion, or for a positive abdominal source; it is not the first step for a pelvic bleed.
D. Internal fixation is definitive, delayed fixation done once the patient is resuscitated and stable; it has no place in the acute management of a hypotensive patient.
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture: binder first, then control the bleeding.
  • Step 1: pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters + blood products
  • Still unstable: angioembolization (arterial bleed) or pre-peritoneal packing
  • External fixation: temporary skeletal stabilization
  • Internal fixation: definitive, once stable
exam_pearl: In a hypotensive pelvic fracture, the simplest bedside device (the binder) beats every operative option as the next step.

stem: A 60 (70) years old Male was found to have inguinal hernia incidentally on physical examination. The hernia is reducible and causes no pain but slight discomfort. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A reducible inguinal hernia in a 60 to 70-year-old man that causes slight discomfort is symptomatic, and the exam rule is that symptomatic inguinal hernias in fit adults are referred for elective surgical repair (open mesh repair for a primary unilateral hernia). Repair relieves symptoms and removes the risk of incarceration and strangulation; the similar recall marked referral for elective repair.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation (watchful waiting) is mainly for a painless hernia, or for a patient who is unfit for or declines surgery; most watched hernias in older men end up needing repair, and this one already causes discomfort.
C. Increasing physical activity does not treat a hernia and may increase intra-abdominal pressure; there is no conservative exercise treatment for an inguinal hernia.
key_concept:
Inguinal hernia management by state and patient.
  • Symptomatic, reducible, fit adult: elective repair (open mesh if primary unilateral)
  • Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair
  • Femoral hernia: repair even if asymptomatic (high strangulation risk)
  • Irreducible tender or obstructed: urgent or emergency surgery
  • Infant umbilical hernia: observe, most close spontaneously
exam_pearl: Even mild discomfort makes an inguinal hernia symptomatic; observation is for a painless hernia in a patient who declines or cannot have surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot of a similar recall (62-year-old man, reducible right inguinal hernia with mild discomfort, Australian guidelines) marks 'B. Referral to a general surgeon for elective repair' (consistent with surgical repair).

stem: 27 YO female presented to OPD with painful swelling in tip of her right thumb 2 days ago, she work as hairdresser and trimming hangnail. Examination show tense tender swelling in pulp of “Nail FOLD Is Intact” which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A tense, tender swelling of the pulp of the thumb tip after minor trauma, with the nail fold intact, is a felon: an abscess in the closed septated compartments of the distal pulp. The key discriminator is location: pulp involvement means felon, whereas infection of the nail fold means paronychia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Paronychia is infection of the nail fold around the nail, classically after trimming a hangnail or manicure; here the stem stresses that the nail fold is intact and the swelling is in the pulp.
C. Onychomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the nail plate causing thickening and discoloration, not an acute tense painful pulp swelling over 2 days.
D. Cellulitis is diffuse, poorly demarcated spreading redness of skin and subcutaneous tissue; a tense, localized pulp swelling is a closed space abscess, which is a felon.
key_concept:
Fingertip infections by site.
  • Felon: pulp space abscess, tense throbbing tip, needs incision and drainage
  • Paronychia: nail fold, often after hangnail or manicure
  • Herpetic whitlow: vesicles, do not incise
  • Flexor tenosynovitis: Kanavel signs, along the whole finger
  • Onychomycosis: chronic nail plate change
exam_pearl: Hangnail history tempts you to paronychia; the words 'pulp' and 'nail fold intact' make it a felon.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: Hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen bulb of the thumb finger after stick injury with a tool. Same options, Felon highlighted.

stem: A Patient with Fatigue, Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain Ca: 3.50 mmol Parathyroid adenoma: 2cm parathyroid adenoma What's Most Appropriate NEXT Step In Management?
why_right: This recall's key is bisphosphonate, read as the immediate step: a calcium of 3.50 mmol/L is markedly raised, at the threshold of severe hypercalcemia, and the acute management is to lower calcium (aggressive IV normal saline, then an IV bisphosphonate) before anything else. The compiler marked this answer with question marks and also flagged parathyroidectomy, so the key is uncertain in the source.
why_wrong_block:
B. A calcimimetic (cinacalcet) lowers PTH and calcium in patients who cannot or will not have surgery, or in parathyroid carcinoma; it is not the first choice in a surgical candidate and acts too slowly for a severe acute rise.
C. Increasing dietary calcium would worsen hypercalcemia and stone formation; it has no role here.
D. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and is clearly indicated (symptomatic disease with renal stones and bone pain, calcium markedly raised, localized adenoma); in this card it is treated as the step after calcium is controlled.
key_concept:
Primary hyperparathyroidism from an adenoma: control severe calcium, then operate.
  • Severe hypercalcemia: IV normal saline first, then IV bisphosphonate (calcitonin for rapid short-term effect)
  • Definitive: parathyroidectomy, after sestamibi localization
  • Surgery indications: any symptomatic PHPT, stones, osteoporosis or fragility fracture, age under 50, calcium well above normal
  • Unfit for surgery: cinacalcet
exam_pearl: If the question says 'definitive management' or omits a high calcium crisis, the answer flips to parathyroidectomy.

Other marked answers: Compiler question-marked: D. Parathyroidectomy ??

stem: (Long scenario) after IV fluid how to confirm that the pt is well resuscitated?
why_right: Adequate resuscitation is shown by restored tissue perfusion, and serum lactate is the most direct marker of it: a lactate of about 2 mmol/L (normal or cleared) means oxygen delivery now meets demand. Among these options it is the only value that confirms successful resuscitation; the source also notes that CVP measures volume, while lactate measures perfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. A CVP of 8 mmHg only estimates intravascular filling; it was an older sepsis target (early goal-directed therapy) but correlates poorly with fluid responsiveness and does not prove the tissues are perfused. The compiler suggested it for a sepsis version, but when lactate is offered, lactate is preferred.
B. A MAP of 45 mmHg is hypotension and indicates ongoing shock; the target is a MAP of at least 65 mmHg.
C. Urine output is an excellent resuscitation marker (classically the best one in burns, target at least 0.5 ml/kg/h in adults), but 0.1 ml/kg/h is severe oliguria and shows inadequate resuscitation.
key_concept:
Endpoints of resuscitation: perfusion beats pressure and volume.
  • Lactate normal or clearing (about 2 mmol/L or less)
  • MAP ≥ 65 mmHg
  • Urine output ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/h adults, ≥ 1 ml/kg/h children (best in burns)
  • Improving mental status and capillary refill
  • CVP: volume estimate only, not an endpoint
exam_pearl: In a burn question that offers an adequate urine output (such as 0.5 to 1 ml/kg/h), choose urine output; here it is 0.1, so lactate wins.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler: If burn case = lactate 2; if Sepsis = CVP 8 (Central Venous Pressure = 8 mmHg). 'If burn case D. Lactate = 2 ✅': lactate reflects tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery; normal or clearing lactate (<2 mmol/L) indicates successful resuscitation, best marker among choices. CVP = volume estimate, lactate = perfusion (more important); CVP 8 is normal but does not confirm adequate resuscitation. Targets: MAP ≥ 65, UO ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/hr (0.1 = severe oliguria), improving mental status, lactate clearance. If choices include CVP vs lactate, pick lactate. Embedded burn recall (40% deep flame burn in ICU, indicator of good response) marks C. Urine output.

stem: Currently presenting with jaundice, and RUQ tenderness. Her LFT and bilirubin are elevated. What is the most appropriate diagnostic imaging?
why_right: This recall's key is MRCP because the lead-in asks for the most appropriate (not the initial) diagnostic imaging: in a patient with jaundice, RUQ tenderness and raised bilirubin and LFTs, MRCP is a non-invasive, accurate way to show the whole biliary tree and detect common bile duct stones or strictures. The compiler stresses the split: initial = ultrasound, most appropriate = MRCP.
why_wrong_block:
B. Abdominal ultrasound is the INITIAL imaging for jaundice with RUQ pain (cheap, quick, shows gallstones and duct dilatation); choose it when the question says 'initial' or 'first'. Its weakness is poor views of the distal CBD.
C. CT abdomen is better for suspected malignant obstruction (pancreatic head mass), complications or staging; it misses many non-calcified CBD stones.
key_concept:
Biliary imaging ladder: read the lead-in verb.
  • Initial: abdominal ultrasound (stones, CBD dilatation)
  • Diagnostic for CBD stones/biliary anatomy: MRCP
  • Therapeutic (stone extraction, stenting): ERCP
  • Suspected malignancy or complications: CT
exam_pearl: 'Initial' or 'first' flips the answer to ultrasound; 'confirm CBD stone' or 'most appropriate' in this recall points to MRCP.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot answer: A. This question comes in multiple formulas: most appropriate INITIAL = US; most appropriate = MRCP. Compiler note: 'It is most appropriate'.

stem: 1 week ago and complaining of mild abdominal pain after the accident. O/E: Vitally stable. Mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant. No other complaints or findings. What is the most appropriate initial step?
OptB: Refer him to emergency department for further evaluation
OptC: Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage
why_right: This recall's key is referral to the emergency department: the patient is being seen outside the ED a week after an accident with new RUQ pain ("after the accident", "mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant"). Even though he is "vitally stable", delayed pain over the liver after trauma can reflect a contained liver injury, subcapsular hematoma or delayed bleeding, so he needs a setting that can image (CT with contrast for the stable patient), monitor serially and intervene if he deteriorates.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound (FAST) is a quick bedside screen for free fluid, mainly in unstable patients; it is operator dependent and poor at grading solid organ injury. In a stable trauma patient the definitive study is CT, and it is done as part of the ED work-up, not as an isolated outpatient test.
C. Blood work (Hb, LFTs) supports the work-up but cannot exclude or localise an injury on its own; a normal early Hb does not rule out bleeding. It would be ordered inside the ED evaluation, not instead of it.
key_concept:
Abdominal trauma work-up depends on hemodynamic status.
  • Unstable + positive FAST: laparotomy
  • Stable blunt trauma: CT abdomen with IV contrast
  • Stable penetrating RUQ wound: CT abdomen
  • Delayed RUQ pain after trauma: think liver injury or subcapsular hematoma
  • Patient seen outside the ED with a possible intra-abdominal injury: send to ED for full evaluation
exam_pearl: If "CT abdomen with contrast" is among the options for a stable trauma patient, it beats both ultrasound and referral.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler: If CT with contrast in choices I will chose it. (Both A and B highlighted; B has ✅.)
Other marked answers: Compiler highlight: A. Do Abdominal ultrasound

stem: 67 year old man 6hours post femoral artery surgery developed swelling and worsening neurological signs (Stem exactly like this)
why_right: This recall's key is the decompression procedure for acute compartment syndrome: "6 hours post femoral artery surgery" with limb "swelling and worsening neurological signs" is classic reperfusion injury after revascularisation. Capillary leak raises compartment pressure, muscle and nerve become ischemic, and irreversible damage follows within hours, so the treatment is emergency release of the fascial compartments (fasciotomy).
why_wrong_block:
A. A backslab (plaster splint) immobilises a fracture; applying any cast or tight dressing to a limb with rising compartment pressure makes it worse. In suspected compartment syndrome all casts and dressings are removed, not added.
B. Traction is used to align or hold fractures (e.g. femoral shaft); it does nothing for compartment pressure and can even raise it.
D. Nerve repair is for a transected nerve. Here the nerve deficit is ischemic from pressure, and it recovers only if the compartment is decompressed promptly.
key_concept:
Post revascularisation swelling + pain + neuro deficit = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
  • Early sign: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch
  • Late signs: paresthesia, paralysis, pallor; pulse may still be present
  • Diagnosis is clinical; compartment pressure measurement if unclear
  • First: remove casts and dressings, keep limb at heart level
  • Definitive: emergency fasciotomy of all involved compartments
exam_pearl: A palpable distal pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome; do not wait for pulselessness.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler: 'fasciotomy ??'. Suspect acute compartment syndrome due to reperfusion injury after vascular surgery: capillary leak increases compartment pressure; muscle and nerve ischemia cause neurologic deficits; permanent damage within 6-8 hours. Emergency fasciotomy to decompress compartments and restore perfusion. Post vascular surgery + pain/swelling + neuro deficit = compartment syndrome: Fasciotomy (cutting open the fascia to relieve pressure inside a muscle compartment; saves the limb).

stem: A patient presents with an open femur fracture with a 5-cm wound. What is the first step in management?
OptB: IV antibiotics within the first hour
why_right: An "open femur fracture with a 5-cm wound" is contaminated from the moment of injury, and the single most effective step against deep infection and osteomyelitis is early IV antibiotics. The lead in is "first step", so antibiotics within the first hour (with tetanus cover, wound photo, saline dressing and splinting) come before the trip to theatre.
why_wrong_block: A. Surgical debridement and irrigation is essential but is the next step, done urgently (within about 12 hours for high energy injuries such as an open femur, within 24 hours for others, immediately for gross contamination) after antibiotics have been started. It would be the answer if the stem says antibiotics are already given and asks for the next step.
key_concept:
Open fracture sequence: antibiotics first, then theatre.
  • 1: ATLS assessment, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, tetanus prophylaxis
  • 2: Photograph wound, cover with saline soaked dressing, splint/reduce
  • 3: Formal debridement and irrigation in theatre
  • 4: Fixation (IM nail if stable patient; external fixator for damage control or heavy contamination)
  • Any wound over a fracture, even 1 cm, = open fracture
exam_pearl: Read the lead in: "first step" = antibiotics; "antibiotics given, next step" = surgical debridement.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another version (Q:): patient fell from a high place and developed a 5 cm thigh wound with dirt. What will you do? A. Wound clean B. Blood transfusion (no answer marked for this version).

stem: A diabetic patient presents with a well-demarcated plantar foot ulcer. The patient has nearly diminished sensation and intact peripheral pulses. The ulcer shows central erythema with signs of healing. What is the most critical test to perform to reach the diagnosis?
why_right: A "plantar" ulcer in a diabetic with "diminished sensation" and "intact peripheral pulses" is a neuropathic ulcer: weight bearing site, adequate perfusion, loss of protective sensation. The test that establishes that diagnosis is the 10-g monofilament test, which confirms loss of protective sensation and therefore the neuropathic cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. ABI assesses arterial insufficiency; it is the key test for an ulcer with absent or weak pulses, a non-healing course, or a dorsal, toe tip or heel location. Here pulses are intact and the ulcer is healing (note ABI can be falsely high in diabetics due to calcified vessels).
C. CT does not diagnose the ulcer type; deep infection or osteomyelitis is assessed with X-ray first and MRI, not CT, and only if suspected.
D. Finding pressure points guides offloading and prevention once neuropathy is established; it is management, not the test that makes the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Diabetic foot ulcer: location + pulses + sensation decide the type.
  • Neuropathic: plantar, under metatarsal heads, painless, intact pulses: monofilament test, offloading
  • Arterial: toes, heel, dorsum, painful, absent pulses: ABI then duplex/CT angiography
  • Venous: gaiter area/medial malleolus, intact pulses: venous duplex
  • Suspect osteomyelitis: probe to bone, X-ray, MRI
exam_pearl: Same stem with a malleolar or dorsal non-healing ulcer flips the answer to ABI.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Plantar ulcer + intact pulses + sensory loss = diabetic neuropathic ulcer = monofilament test (10-g monofilament assesses loss of protective sensation). Screenshot versions: examiner says pulse was not mentioned, only diminished sensation; ulcer regular, peri-wound erythema; Answer: B. Other examiners: ulcer on malleoli (Dec) / dorsal not plantar (Apr); if non-healing, malleoli and dorsal locations favor arterial ulcer and answer is ABI. Other marked answers: Screenshot variant (ulcer on malleoli/dorsal, non-healing): A. ABI

stem: What is appropriate after trauma history with decreased pulses and ulceration on arm?
key_concept:
Trauma + limb at risk: decide arterial vs compartment.
  • Hard signs of arterial injury (absent pulse, pallor, cold, expanding hematoma): surgical exploration/repair
  • Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense limb; fasciotomy
  • After revascularisation of prolonged ischemia: consider prophylactic fasciotomy
  • Never elevate an ischemic or compartment-syndrome limb above the heart; keep at heart level
exam_pearl: Pulseless + pale, cold limb after trauma points to the artery (explore); pulseless + severe pain, paresthesia and a tense compartment after a fracture is late compartment syndrome (fasciotomy).

stem: A patient with diabetes presents with swelling of the big toe and warmth and tenderness of the (calf) for 4 days. There is 2 cm ulcer over the first metatarsal area. No discharge is noted. Distal pulses are intact. What is the most appropriate investigation?

Diabetic foot/leg: pick the test for the threat the stem emphasises.
  • Leg ulcer: check pulses first; absent = arterial Doppler, intact = venous duplex
  • Calf warmth/tenderness/swelling: venous duplex for DVT
  • Suspected osteomyelitis: X-ray first, MRI most accurate, bone biopsy definitive
  • Angiography: arterial disease needing revascularisation

stem: 65 years man with reducible inguinal hernia, mild discomfort without significant pain.
why_right: The hernia is "reducible" with only "mild discomfort without significant pain", so it is minimally symptomatic. In an older man with a minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia, watchful waiting with review is an accepted option because the risk of acute incarceration is low; surgery is offered if symptoms increase or the hernia becomes irreducible.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgical repair: right once the hernia is clearly symptomatic (pain limiting activity), enlarging, irreducible, or the patient wants repair; mild discomfort alone does not mandate it.
B. Lifestyle modification: general advice (weight loss, avoid straining) may accompany follow-up but is not itself a management plan for the hernia.
C. Activity modification: does not treat or monitor the hernia; restricting activity is not required and would fit only as supportive advice, not the chosen strategy.
key_concept:
Inguinal hernia management depends on symptoms and state.
  • Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, reducible (adult man): watchful waiting is acceptable
  • Symptomatic: elective repair (open mesh for primary unilateral)
  • Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair
  • Femoral hernia: repair even if asymptomatic
  • Tender, irreducible, obstructed or strangulated: emergency surgery
exam_pearl: "Mild discomfort" = watch; "pain limiting activity", irreducible, or femoral = repair.

stem: Man who experienced a road traffic accident (RTA), had a lucid interval, and then lost consciousness, with a convex lesion found on CT scan. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Head trauma with a "lucid interval" followed by loss of consciousness and a "convex" (lens shaped, biconvex) lesion on CT is an epidural hematoma, usually from a torn middle meningeal artery. This is an expanding arterial bleed causing mass effect, so the definitive and most appropriate management is urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the hematoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Shunt: a ventriculoperitoneal shunt treats hydrocephalus; it does not remove an extradural clot compressing the brain.
C. Mannitol: a temporizing measure to lower intracranial pressure while arranging surgery; it does not stop the arterial bleed or remove the hematoma.
D. Intubation: protects the airway when GCS is 8 or less and is done as part of ABC resuscitation, but it is supportive; the question asks for the management of the lesion itself, which is surgical evacuation.
key_concept:
Epidural vs subdural hematoma.
  • Epidural: convex, lens shaped; middle meningeal artery; lucid interval; often temporal fracture
  • Subdural: concave, crescent shaped; bridging veins; elderly, alcoholics, gradual
  • Symptomatic epidural hematoma: urgent craniotomy and evacuation
  • Mannitol and intubation are bridges, not definitive treatment
exam_pearl: Lens (convex) + lucid interval = epidural; the answer is craniotomy, with airway and mannitol only as bridges.

stem: Patient was involved in a motor vehicle accident and presents with Paradoxical chest wall movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: "Paradoxical chest wall movement" after blunt trauma means a segment of the chest wall has lost bony continuity: flail chest, from several adjacent ribs each fractured in two or more places. The free segment is sucked in on inspiration and pushed out on expiration.
why_wrong_block: B. Cardiac contusion: presents with arrhythmias, new ECG changes or hypotension after a sternal blow; it does not cause paradoxical movement of the chest wall.
key_concept:
Chest trauma pattern recognition.
  • Paradoxical movement: flail chest
  • Flail chest treatment: analgesia, oxygen, assisted ventilation if hypoxic
  • Hyperresonance, tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension: tension pneumothorax
  • Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds, equal air entry: cardiac tamponade
  • Arrhythmia or ECG changes after sternal impact: cardiac contusion
exam_pearl: The hypoxia in flail chest comes mainly from the underlying pulmonary contusion, not the loose segment itself.

stem: A hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen bulb of the thumb finger after getting a stick from the tools she's using. Nail bed is intact.
highlight_terms_source: swollen bulb of the thumb finger
why_right: A swollen, tense "bulb" (pulp) of the thumb after a puncture ("a stick from the tools") with the "nail bed" intact is a felon: an infection of the closed septated pulp space of the distal phalanx, usually Staphylococcus aureus introduced by penetrating injury. The septa make it a tense, very painful collection that needs incision and drainage if pus has formed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Paronychia: infection of the nail fold at the side or base of the nail, typically after nail biting or manicure; here the nail region is spared and the pulp is affected.
C. Onychomycosis: a chronic fungal infection causing thick, discoloured, crumbling nails, not an acute painful pulp swelling after a puncture.
D. Cellulitis: diffuse spreading erythema of skin and subcutaneous tissue without a tense loculated collection; the localized tense pulp swelling points to a felon.
key_concept:
Fingertip infections by location.
  • Pulp of distal phalanx, tense, after puncture: felon (incision and drainage)
  • Nail fold: paronychia
  • Vesicles on fingertip, herpes exposure: herpetic whitlow (do NOT incise)
  • Fusiform swollen finger, flexed posture, pain on passive extension: flexor tenosynovitis
  • Chronic thick discoloured nail: onychomycosis
exam_pearl: Pulp = felon, nail fold = paronychia, vesicles = herpetic whitlow which must not be incised.

stem: Child presents with a distal radius fracture. On examination, there is swelling, redness, pain, and paresthesia of the hand. Distal pulses are intact. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: After a forearm fracture, swelling, pain and "paresthesia of the hand" indicate rising compartment pressure with nerve ischemia: compartment syndrome. Pain and paresthesia are early signs, whereas pulselessness is very late, so "distal pulses are intact" does not exclude it. Treatment of compartment syndrome is urgent fasciotomy, which can proceed on clinical suspicion alone.
why_wrong_block: B. Elevation of the hand: fits a simple swollen fracture without neurovascular signs; in suspected compartment syndrome elevation lowers arterial perfusion pressure, so the limb is kept at heart level and decompressed.
key_concept:
Compartment syndrome = clinical diagnosis, treated by urgent fasciotomy.
  • Earliest sign: pain out of proportion, worse on passive stretch
  • Then paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis
  • Palpable pulses do NOT exclude it
  • First remove any cast or tight dressing; keep limb at heart level
  • Compartment pressure above 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis but is not required
exam_pearl: Intact pulses are a trap: pulselessness is a late sign, so pain plus paresthesia after a fracture already means fasciotomy.

stem: Patient came to your clinic today; he mentioned he had an RTA 1 week ago and is complaining of mild abdominal pain after the accident. O/E: Vitally stable. Mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant. No other complaints or findings. What is the most appropriate initial step?
OptB: Refer him to emergency department for further evaluation
OptC: Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage
key_concept:
Delayed abdominal pain after blunt trauma: decide by stability.
  • Abnormal vitals or worsening pain: send to ED (a variant of this recall with abnormal vitals is keyed to referral)
  • Stable with normal vitals: imaging (ultrasound, CT in ED) to exclude liver or splenic injury
  • RUQ pain after trauma: think liver laceration or subcapsular hematoma, which can bleed late
  • Blood tests support but never exclude bleeding
exam_pearl: Stability decides: any abnormal vital, worsening pain or peritonism makes ED referral right; only a fully stable patient with a benign abdomen can be imaged as an outpatient.

stem: Patient came to outpatient clinic; he had an RTA 1 week ago and complains of mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant. No other complaints or findings. Vitals were written in numbers; however, some vitals were abnormal. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptB: Refer him to emergency department for further evaluation
OptC: Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage
why_right: A patient with post-traumatic RUQ pain ("RTA 1 week ago") in an outpatient clinic whose "vitals were abnormal" may be bleeding from a delayed liver or other solid organ injury. He needs resuscitation capability, serial assessment and a trauma work-up (usually CT if he stabilizes), which only the emergency department can provide, so the most appropriate next step is referral to the ED.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal ultrasound: reasonable in a fully stable patient with normal vitals; with abnormal vitals, arranging imaging from the clinic delays resuscitation and definitive assessment.
C. Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage: hemoglobin may be normal early in acute bleeding, so labs cannot exclude hemorrhage; they are an adjunct done in the ED, not the next step.
key_concept:
Post-trauma abdominal pain in clinic: stability decides.
  • Abnormal vitals: refer to ED (resuscitation, trauma work-up)
  • Normal vitals, mild pain: outpatient imaging may be considered
  • Unstable trauma patient in ED: FAST then laparotomy if positive
  • Stable trauma patient in ED: CT abdomen with contrast
exam_pearl: The single word "abnormal" in the vitals moves the answer from outpatient imaging to ED referral.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant of 354 ('Same above, vitals were written in numbers. HOWEVER, some vitals were abnormal').

stem: A 36-year-old male presents to the emergency room with right abdominal pain. On examination, he is febrile, toxic, and has tenderness in the right upper quadrant and lower intercostal margins. He reports anorexia and weight loss. Laboratory findings: elevated temperature (~37.9°C), high WBC count, elevated bilirubin. Ultrasound: cystic lesion with thick wall in the liver. What is the most appropriate step in management? (I am sure it was not 'next')
highlight_terms_source: cystic lesion with thick wall in the liver
why_right: A "febrile, toxic" patient with RUQ tenderness, leukocytosis, raised bilirubin and a "cystic lesion with thick wall in the liver" has a liver abscess, and with no travel, dysentery or amoebic serology the picture is that of a pyogenic abscess. Pyogenic abscess is treated by draining the pus plus antibiotics; the least invasive effective drainage is image-guided percutaneous drainage, which is the key step here (the lead-in is "most appropriate", not "next").
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone: antibiotics are given alongside drainage, but antibiotics alone rarely cure an established pyogenic abscess in a toxic patient; alone they fit only very small abscesses.
B. Metronidazole: the initial treatment if the abscess is amoebic (travel to an endemic area, dysentery, positive Entamoeba serology), even when large; those clues are absent here.
C. Surgical drainage: reserved for failed or impossible percutaneous drainage, rupture with peritonitis, or a concurrent surgical cause; it is more invasive than needed as the first approach.
key_concept:
Liver abscess: identify the type, then treat.
  • Pyogenic (toxic, often biliary source): percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics
  • Amoebic (travel, dysentery, positive serology): metronidazole first, drain only if no response or impending rupture
  • Hydatid (daughter cysts, Echinococcus): albendazole, then PAIR or surgery
  • Open surgical drainage: failure of percutaneous route or rupture
exam_pearl: If the stem gives amoebic clues (travel, bloody diarrhea, positive ELISA), metronidazole becomes the answer even for a large abscess.

stem: A 55 YO male underwent PTC (percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography) for obstructive jaundice. After 24 hours of the procedure he developed hematemesis. His vitals are stable. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Hematemesis 24 hours after PTC means hemobilia until proven otherwise: the transhepatic needle injures a hepatic vessel and blood drains through the bile duct into the duodenum. This recall's key is upper GI endoscopy because the patient is stable and the lead-in is the next step: endoscopy is the first-line test for any hematemesis, rules out common causes such as ulcer or varices, and may show blood coming from the ampulla of Vater, which confirms a biliary source.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT abdomen (CT angiography) can suggest a hepatic pseudoaneurysm, but it is not the first test for hematemesis and cannot treat the bleed.
C. US may show clot in the bile ducts but has poor sensitivity for the bleeding vessel and cannot stop it; it is not how hematemesis is worked up.
D. Angiography is the gold standard for diagnosing hemobilia and allows embolization in the same session; it becomes the answer when bleeding is ongoing, the patient is unstable, or endoscopy points to a biliary source.
key_concept:
Bleeding after a hepatobiliary procedure (PTC, liver biopsy, TIPS, drain, ERCP) = think hemobilia.
  • Classic triad: RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding
  • About half of hemobilia is iatrogenic
  • Stable + hematemesis + lead-in 'next step': upper GI endoscopy (exclude ulcer/varices, see blood at the ampulla)
  • Gold standard diagnosis and treatment: angiography with transarterial embolization
  • Vessel lesion: usually pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula
exam_pearl: The same PTC stem with low Hb and borderline vitals (AS-0370) is keyed to angiography; this stable variant is keyed to endoscopy, so read the vitals and the lead-in.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler flagged 'this question needs re-correction'; MG answer is D (noted in Arabic as the one to memorize even if wrong). Explanation: PTC can cause hemobilia (hepatic vessel injury, blood via bile duct to duodenum; Quincke triad RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding). Pt hemodynamically stable, best initial diagnostic step is Upper GI endoscopy: first-line for hematemesis, can show blood from ampulla of Vater, excludes ulcer/varices. CT not first line; US low sensitivity; angiography after diagnosis or if bleeding persists (embolization). Post-hepatobiliary procedure + hematemesis = hemobilia, first test endoscopy; definitive = angiography with embolization.
Other marked answers: MedGard: D. Angiography

stem: A 73-year-old woman underwent percutaneous trans-hepatic cholangiography for treatment of obstructive jaundice. 24 hours after the procedure, she started to have upper gastrointestinal bleeding (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management plan? BP 105/62 mmHg, HR 89/min, RR 22/min, O2 sat 94%. Hb 103 g/L (normal 130-170 male, 120-160 female), WBC 7.8 x 10^9/L.
why_right: Upper GI bleeding 24 hours after percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is hemobilia: the procedure injures an intrahepatic artery (often a pseudoaneurysm) that bleeds into the biliary tree. Angiography is the gold standard to localize the bleeding vessel and allows transarterial embolization in the same session. The low Hb (103 g/L), raised RR and borderline BP show significant blood loss, which favors going straight to the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic test.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT scan (CT angiography) may suggest a pseudoaneurysm but is not the gold standard and cannot treat; conventional angiography does both.
B. Endoscopy may show blood coming from the ampulla but cannot localize or control an intrahepatic arterial source; it is the first test for ordinary upper GI bleeding without a preceding liver procedure.
C. Ultrasound may show clot in the bile ducts but cannot identify or treat the bleeding vessel.
key_concept:
Upper GI bleeding after PTC, liver biopsy, TIPS or other hepatobiliary procedure = hemobilia.
  • Triad: RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding
  • About 50% of hemobilia is iatrogenic
  • Gold standard: angiography
  • First-line treatment: transarterial embolization in the same session
  • Ordinary UGIB without hepatobiliary procedure: endoscopy first
exam_pearl: The procedure history (PTC, liver biopsy) is what moves the answer from endoscopy to angiography.
compiler_note: Compiler note: D marked ✅✅ MG (MedGard). Compare 369 (stable vitals variant, compiler favored endoscopy).

stem: DM patient came with dental infection and subsequently develops jaundice and chills. Ultrasound reveals a 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver
why_right: A diabetic with a dental infection who then develops chills and jaundice with a 6 cm hypoechoic liver lesion has a pyogenic liver abscess from hematogenous spread of oral flora. Large pyogenic abscesses need source control: image-guided percutaneous drainage (catheter or aspiration) combined with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, which is the most appropriate initial management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral antibiotics alone do not penetrate a large walled-off collection and are inadequate for a septic patient; antibiotics alone (IV) suit only small abscesses, and an amoebic abscess is the one treated with metronidazole without drainage.
C. Antifungals and follow up fit hepatosplenic candidiasis in neutropenic patients (multiple small lesions), not a single large abscess after a dental source.
key_concept:
Liver abscess: identify the type, then treat.
  • Pyogenic (biliary disease, bacteremia from dental or abdominal source, diabetes): IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage for large abscesses
  • Amoebic (travel, dysentery, solitary lesion, positive serology): metronidazole first; drainage only if it fails or rupture is imminent
  • Hydatid (Echinococcus): albendazole, then drainage or surgery for large/complicated cysts
  • Surgery: rupture, failed percutaneous drainage, or multiloculated abscess
exam_pearl: Travel plus dysentery points to amoebic abscess and metronidazole alone; a bacterial source (teeth, biliary tree) plus a large abscess means drainage.

stem: Patient had MVA and was stable, (I think after 2 days) had shortness of breath; chest examination: decreased breath sounds and dullness on percussion on one side of the chest, also hypotensive. Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: decreased breath sounds and dullness on percussion
why_right: After an MVA, the patient develops dyspnea with decreased breath sounds and DULLNESS to percussion on one side plus hypotension: fluid (blood) in the pleural space with blood loss. That is a hemothorax, and a delayed presentation after initially being stable is well recognized, as slow bleeding from fractured ribs or intercostal vessels gradually fills the chest.
why_wrong_block:
B. Tension pneumothorax also gives absent breath sounds and hypotension, but the chest is HYPERRESONANT, with tracheal deviation away and distended neck veins, and it develops acutely.
C. Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia with patchy infiltrates but no unilateral dullness or effusion; cardiac contusion causes arrhythmias or pump failure, not unilateral chest signs.
D. Cardiac tamponade gives hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds with EQUAL breath sounds on both sides (Beck triad).
key_concept:
Chest trauma + hypotension: let percussion decide.
  • Dull + decreased breath sounds = hemothorax (chest tube; neck veins flat)
  • Hyperresonant + decreased breath sounds + tracheal shift + raised JVP = tension pneumothorax (needle decompression then chest tube)
  • Equal breath sounds + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds = tamponade (pericardiocentesis/surgery)
  • Thoracotomy for hemothorax: initial chest tube output over 1500 mL, or ongoing 200 to 300 mL per hour for several hours
exam_pearl: Dull = blood, hyperresonant = air; the percussion note is the one word that flips hemothorax and tension pneumothorax.

stem: A patient with fatigue, recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain. Ca: 3.50 mmol. 2 cm parathyroid adenoma. What's the most appropriate NEXT step in management? No polyuria, polydipsia, no CNS symptoms.
highlight_terms_source: recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain
key_concept:
Symptomatic PHPT = parathyroidectomy; very high calcium = stabilize first.
  • Surgery indications: any symptoms (stones, fractures, bone pain), Ca ≥1 mg/dL above ULN, osteoporosis or fragility fracture, age <50, renal involvement (stones, nephrocalcinosis, GFR <60)
  • Localize before surgery: sestamibi scan (with neck US)
  • Acute severe hypercalcemia ladder: IV normal saline, then calcitonin (fast), then IV bisphosphonate (slower, longer acting)
  • Cinacalcet: when surgery is not possible
exam_pearl: 'Most appropriate' = parathyroidectomy; 'NEXT step' with a very high calcium = lower it first (fluids if offered, otherwise bisphosphonate).

Other marked answers: Compiler typed 'Answer: D or A ??'; D. Parathyroidectomy if asked 'most appropriate' (not 'next')

stem: Patient known case of diverticulosis presented with mild and intermittent pain left lower quadrant. How to manage?
why_right: A known case of diverticulosis with only mild, intermittent LLQ pain and no features of inflammation is symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease, not diverticulitis. Management is outpatient: a high-fiber diet (with adequate fluids) softens stool and lowers intracolonic pressure, reducing symptoms and future episodes.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT abdomen is right when diverticulitis is suspected (constant LLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis, tenderness) to stage it and look for abscess or perforation; intermittent mild pain does not need it.
B. IV antibiotics are for complicated or severe diverticulitis (abscess, systemic illness, unable to tolerate oral intake); there is no infection here.
key_concept:
Diverticular disease ladder:
  • Diverticulosis, asymptomatic or mild intermittent pain: high-fiber diet and fluids
  • Suspected diverticulitis (LLQ pain, fever, high WBC): CT abdomen with contrast
  • Uncomplicated diverticulitis: outpatient care, antibiotics selectively
  • Abscess: IV antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage
  • Generalized peritonitis/perforation: emergency surgery (Hartmann procedure)
exam_pearl: Fever, leukocytosis or constant localized tenderness turn diverticulosis into diverticulitis and move the answer to CT.

stem: Old man known case of diverticulosis, came complaining of mild intermittent left lower abdominal pain, has no fever, normal WBCs and no signs of peritonitis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: no fever, normal WBCs and no signs of peritonitis
why_right: The stem removes every feature of diverticulitis: no fever, normal WBCs, no signs of peritonitis, and the pain is mild and intermittent. This is symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease, so the most appropriate initial management is increasing fiber and fluid intake to soften stool and lower colonic pressure.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT abdomen is the test for suspected acute diverticulitis (fever, leukocytosis, localized tenderness); none are present here.
B. IV antibiotics and bowel rest are for complicated or severe diverticulitis (abscess, systemic toxicity, cannot tolerate oral intake), not for uninflamed diverticulosis.
D. Laparotomy is reserved for perforated diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis or failure of conservative treatment; this abdomen is soft.
key_concept:
Diverticular disease: match the treatment to inflammation.
  • No fever, normal WBC, no peritonism: high fiber + fluids
  • Suspected diverticulitis: CT with contrast
  • Complicated (abscess): IV antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage
  • Purulent or fecal peritonitis: emergency surgery
exam_pearl: Normal WBC and no fever are the clues that this is diverticulosis, not diverticulitis; do not order CT or antibiotics.

stem: 28 years old female came to the clinic complaining of on and off painless rectal bleeding; she had anal swelling that reduced spontaneously. Anoscopy showed hemorrhoids on 3, 7, 11 o'clock with active bleeding. Labs showed anemia, hemoglobin 8.8. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Painless bleeding with prolapse and anoscopy showing hemorrhoids at the classic 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions confirms internal hemorrhoids. This recall's key is hemorrhoidectomy because the hemorrhoids are actively bleeding and have already caused anemia (Hb 8.8), a complicated picture where definitive excision is chosen over observation or office procedures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Follow up alone is never enough for hemorrhoids that are actively bleeding and causing anemia.
B. Conservative treatment (fiber, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths) is right for external hemorrhoids and uncomplicated grade I to II internal hemorrhoids without anemia.
C. Rubber band ligation is the office procedure for grade I to III internal hemorrhoids that fail conservative care; it is the usual next step for bleeding grade II piles without significant anemia.
key_concept:
Internal hemorrhoids by grade:
  • Grade I (no prolapse) and II (reduce spontaneously): conservative
  • Grade III (manual reduction): rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared coagulation
  • Grade IV (irreducible or thrombosed): hemorrhoidectomy
  • Escalate: failed conservative care, then office procedure, then surgery
  • Most common complication after hemorrhoidectomy: urinary retention
exam_pearl: Spontaneous reduction makes these grade II, which alone would point to conservative care or banding; the anemia and active bleeding are what the key uses to justify surgery.

stem: A patient presents with an open fracture. What is the initial management?
why_right: For an open fracture, the lead-in asks for the initial management. After the ATLS primary survey, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (with tetanus prophylaxis) are started in the emergency department as early as possible, ideally within the first hour, because delay to the first antibiotic dose raises the risk of deep infection. Sterile dressing and splinting follow, then debridement in theatre.
why_wrong_block:
A. Compression (direct pressure) is the first move only when there is active external hemorrhage from the wound; the stem describes no bleeding.
B. Analgesia and fluids are supportive and are part of resuscitation, but they are the answer only when the stem shows shock; they do not address the infection risk that defines open fracture care.
D. Surgical debridement and stabilization is the definitive step, done urgently in theatre after antibiotics; it becomes the answer when antibiotics are already given or the question asks for the next or definitive step.
key_concept:
Open fracture sequence:
  • ATLS primary survey; control hemorrhage with direct pressure if bleeding
  • IV antibiotics as early as possible (within 1 hour) + tetanus prophylaxis
  • Sterile saline-soaked dressing, splint, photograph wound
  • Urgent irrigation and debridement in theatre
  • Definitive fixation (e.g. intramedullary nail or external fixator)
exam_pearl: 'Antibiotics already given' or 'devitalized tissue and dirt, next step' flips the answer to surgical debridement.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Both A and C carried '??'; C's '??' highlighted. Compiler: needs a double check. ATLS: primary survey, then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately (ideally within 1 hour), tetanus prophylaxis, sterile dressing and immobilization, urgent surgical debridement and fixation.

stem: Patient with trauma to the thigh, about 4 cm wound with visible underlying tissues and bone. What is the initial treatment?
OptC: IV antibiotics within the first hour
why_right: A 4 cm thigh wound with visible underlying tissue and bone is an open fracture (bone exposed through the wound). The initial treatment is IV broad-spectrum antibiotics given within the first hour (plus tetanus prophylaxis), because early antibiotics are a key factor in preventing deep infection. Dressing, splinting and urgent debridement follow.
why_wrong_block:
A. A compressive dressing is right when the wound is actively bleeding (direct pressure is the first step for external hemorrhage); the stem mentions no bleeding, so the open fracture priority is antibiotics.
B. Analgesia and fluids support the patient and are given when there is pain or shock, but they are not the specific initial treatment of an open fracture.
D. Surgical debridement and stabilization is the definitive step after antibiotics; it is chosen when the question asks for the next step once antibiotics are running.
key_concept:
Open fracture: antibiotics first, theatre second.
  • Primary survey; direct pressure for active bleeding
  • IV antibiotics within 1 hour + tetanus
  • Sterile dressing and splint
  • Urgent irrigation and debridement
  • Definitive fixation
exam_pearl: This stem has a duplicate keyed to compressive dressing (AS-0794); that answer only wins if the wound is described as bleeding.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0794 → A. Apply a compressive dressing. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: A and C both marked '??'; C highlighted. Needs a double check. ATLS: early IV antibiotics essential in all open fractures, ideally within 1 hour; then sterile dressing, splinting, tetanus prophylaxis, then urgent irrigation and debridement.

stem: pt after MVC come with low bp and maybe tachycardia what is initial step
OptA: iv fluid intervention (like this i dont remember)
key_concept:
Trauma + hypotension = hemorrhage until proven otherwise; restore volume and control bleeding before any vasopressor.
  • Hypovolemic (tachycardia, cold peripheries): IV access, fluid/blood, find and stop the bleed
  • Neurogenic (bradycardia, warm, spinal injury): fluids first, then vasopressor
  • Obstructive (distended neck veins): tamponade or tension pneumothorax, decompress
  • Vasopressors only after adequate volume, in distributive shock
exam_pearl: Tachycardia points to blood loss and volume first; hypotension with bradycardia after spinal injury is the scenario where a vasopressor enters early.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 26 years old primigravida presented 10 days after vaginal delivery complaining of fever and back pain. On examination, lower back tenderness lower limb weakness, and incontinence. Diagnosis of spinal epidural abscess was made. Most appropriate management?
why_right: Spinal epidural abscess with an established neurological deficit (lower limb weakness and incontinence) is a surgical emergency: urgent surgical decompression and drainage, combined with IV antibiotics, gives the best chance of neurological recovery. The recent obstetric epidural is the likely route of infection, and fever with focal back tenderness completes the classic picture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics are always given, but antibiotics alone are reserved for patients with no neurological deficit or who are unfit for surgery; with weakness and sphincter loss, delaying decompression risks permanent paralysis.
C. Image-guided needle aspiration is an option only in selected patients without deficit (or poor surgical candidates); it cannot decompress a cord or cauda equina already compromised.
D. Observation wastes the time window; any new or progressing deficit in epidural abscess needs urgent decompression.
key_concept:
Spinal epidural abscess: fever + focal back pain/tenderness + neurological deficit; MRI with contrast confirms.
  • Risk: recent epidural/spinal procedure, IV drug use, diabetes, bacteremia
  • Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Neurological deficit present: urgent surgical decompression + IV antibiotics
  • No deficit or unfit for surgery: IV antibiotics ± image-guided aspiration with close neuro monitoring
exam_pearl: The moment weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction appears, the answer moves from antibiotics to surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: 'Patient delivered with epidural anesthesia, after 1 week she presented to ED with low back pain with lower paresis and bowel dysfunction, it was abscess. What to do?' A. Surgical drainage (highlighted) B. Needle aspiration.

stem: A 42-year-old woman involved in a head on collision arrived at the Emergency Room talking coherently, with the following vital signs. Her examination revealed equal air entry bilaterally with ecchymosis on her anterior chest wall, distended neck veins and her abdomen is soft and lax. Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, Heart rate 130/min, Respiratory rate 18/min Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: ecchymosis on her anterior chest wall
why_right: After blunt chest trauma (anterior chest wall ecchymosis), the patient has distended neck veins and hypotension (90/60) with tachycardia: two parts of Beck triad, which is enough to call cardiac tamponade. Equal air entry bilaterally with a normal respiratory rate argues against the other obstructive cause, tension pneumothorax, and the soft abdomen makes intra-abdominal bleeding less likely.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cardiac contusion usually presents with arrhythmias or ECG changes (and troponin rise); it does not explain raised neck veins with clear, equal lungs as well as tamponade does.
C. Massive hemothorax gives reduced air entry and dullness on one side, with flat neck veins from blood loss; here air entry is equal and veins are distended.
D. Tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal shift; a bilateral one would leave her in severe respiratory distress with silent chests, not talking comfortably with RR 18 and normal air entry on both sides.
key_concept:
Distended neck veins + hypotension after chest trauma = obstructive shock; breath sounds decide which one.
  • Equal air entry, (muffled heart sounds): cardiac tamponade, treat with pericardiocentesis / surgical drainage
  • Absent breath sounds, hyperresonant, trachea shifted: tension pneumothorax, needle decompression then chest tube
  • Dull, reduced air entry, flat neck veins: massive hemothorax, chest tube ± thoracotomy
  • Beck triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
exam_pearl: Raised JVP with equal air entry is tamponade; raised JVP with one silent hemithorax is tension pneumothorax.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related 'Q:' version: patient stabbed in chest with hypotension, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, clear lungs; options Myocardial contusion / Hemothorax / Tension pneumothorax / Cardiac tamponade; Answer: D. Cardiac tamponade.

stem: Woman has long-standing right upper side pain. Imaging showed about 4 cm polypoid lesion. What is the best management?
why_right: Gallbladder polyps are managed by size, risk factors and symptoms. A 4 cm polypoid lesion is far beyond the 10 mm threshold for cholecystectomy and carries a real risk of malignancy, and the long-standing right upper pain is an additional indication on its own. Cholecystectomy (with oncological planning if malignancy is suspected on imaging) is the answer.
why_wrong_block: B. Conservative management (ultrasound surveillance) is for small asymptomatic polyps: 6 to 9 mm without risk factors, or ≤5 mm with a risk factor. A 4 cm symptomatic lesion must be removed.
key_concept:
Gallbladder polyp: decide by size, risk factors, growth and symptoms.
  • ≥10 mm: cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm + ≥1 risk factor: cholecystectomy
  • Growth ≥2 mm within 2 years: cholecystectomy
  • Unexplained gallbladder symptoms (RUQ pain): cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm without risk factors, or ≤5 mm with a risk factor: ultrasound surveillance over 2 years
exam_pearl: Symptoms alone justify cholecystectomy for a polyp, whatever its size; size ≥10 mm justifies it even without symptoms.

stem: A 35-year-old woman had abdominal ultrasound as part of screening for essential hypertension. She has no abdominal symptoms (see report). Ultrasound Abdomen: Gall bladder single polyp measures 0.6 cm, no stones, and normal bile ducts. Which is the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is surgical consultation for an incidental single 0.6 cm gallbladder polyp in an asymptomatic 35-year-old with no stones and normal ducts. The reasoning behind the key is that any true polyp carries some malignant potential and a surgeon should assess whether removal or surveillance is appropriate. Note that size-based guidance places this polyp in the surveillance group (see concern).
why_wrong_block:
B. A 6 to 9 mm polyp cannot simply be ignored; at minimum it needs ultrasound surveillance for growth. No follow-up is acceptable only for very small polyps without risk factors.
C. Liver function tests do not guide polyp management; the decision rests on polyp size, malignancy risk factors, growth and symptoms. The ducts are already normal on ultrasound.
D. Not the keyed answer here, although it is what size-based guidance recommends for a 6 to 9 mm polyp with no risk factors: repeat ultrasound to detect growth.
key_concept:
Gallbladder polyp management by size and risk.
  • ≥10 mm: cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm + ≥1 risk factor: cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm, no risk factors: ultrasound surveillance over 2 years
  • Growth ≥2 mm within 2 years or unexplained RUQ symptoms: cholecystectomy
  • Risk factors include older age, primary sclerosing cholangitis, Indian ethnicity, sessile polyp
exam_pearl: Exam key for this exact recall is surgical consultation; if the options make you choose by guideline size cut-offs, 6 to 9 mm without risk factors means follow-up ultrasound.

stem: Patient came to outpatient clinic today he mentioned he had an RTA 1 week ago and complaining of mild abdominal pain after accident. O/E: Vitally stable. Mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant. No other complaints or findings. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptB: Refer him to emergency department for further evaluation
OptC: Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage
why_right: A vitally stable outpatient with only mild RUQ pain one week after an RTA and no other findings needs a non-invasive look for a delayed or missed solid organ injury (liver laceration, subcapsular hematoma, contained collection). Abdominal ultrasound is quick, radiation-free, available in clinic and appropriate as the next step in a stable patient; abnormal findings or deterioration then lead to CT and admission.
why_wrong_block:
B. ED referral is right if the patient is unstable, has peritonitis, worsening pain or abnormal findings; this patient is stable with mild pain, so an immediate ED transfer is not the most appropriate first step.
C. Blood tests (Hb, LFT) may support but cannot localize or exclude an organ injury; a normal Hb a week later does not rule out a hematoma, so imaging is the decisive step.
key_concept:
Abdominal pain after blunt trauma: hemodynamic status decides the pathway.
  • Unstable + free fluid on FAST: laparotomy
  • Stable: CT abdomen with contrast is the definitive test in the acute setting
  • Stable outpatient with mild late pain: ultrasound first, escalate to CT if abnormal
  • Delayed splenic/hepatic rupture can present days after trauma
exam_pearl: Stability is the switch: stable patient gets imaging, unstable patient gets the operating room or emergency department.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q (other version): vitals were given as numbers in a large table, all within normal range; same options, A highlighted.

stem: 45-year-old patient who was incidentally found on ultrasound (US) to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) measuring 4.5 cm. What to do?
why_right: An incidental, asymptomatic 4.5 cm AAA is below the elective repair threshold (5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women). Below that size the risk of rupture is lower than the risk of operating, so the aneurysm is followed with serial ultrasound, together with risk factor control (smoking cessation, BP and lipid control).
why_wrong_block: A. Immediate surgery is for a ruptured or symptomatic (tender, painful) aneurysm; elective repair is for diameter above the threshold or rapid growth. A 4.5 cm asymptomatic AAA meets none of these.
key_concept:
AAA: size, symptoms and growth decide.
  • Initial imaging and surveillance: ultrasound
  • Confirm/plan (stable, symptomatic or before repair or other abdominal surgery): CT angiography
  • Asymptomatic, below threshold: surveillance + risk factor control
  • Repair: ≥5.5 cm men, ≥5 cm women, growth >1 cm/year, symptomatic or ruptured
exam_pearl: Any pain, tenderness or rupture overrides size: a symptomatic AAA of any diameter goes for repair.

stem: 70 years old known HTN and smoker on routine check up found Aortic Aneurism 4.5 cm. What is the management?
why_right: A 4.5 cm aneurysm found on routine check-up (asymptomatic) in a 70-year-old is below the repair threshold (5.5 cm in men, 5 cm in women), so the answer is ultrasound surveillance with risk factor control, here stopping smoking and controlling his hypertension. Surveillance intervals vary between guidelines; the principle is regular imaging to detect growth.
why_wrong_block:
B. EVAR is a method of repair, used once repair is indicated (≥5.5 cm, growth >1 cm/year, symptoms or rupture) and anatomy is suitable; not indicated at 4.5 cm.
C. Open surgical repair has the same indications as EVAR (often chosen in younger, fit patients or unsuitable anatomy); below threshold its operative risk outweighs rupture risk.
key_concept:
AAA below threshold = watch; above threshold, symptomatic or fast-growing = repair (EVAR or open).
  • Repair threshold: ≥5.5 cm men, ≥5 cm women
  • Rapid growth >1 cm/year: repair
  • Symptomatic or ruptured: repair regardless of size
  • Below threshold: ultrasound surveillance, stop smoking, BP and lipid control
exam_pearl: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA growth; stopping it is part of the answer when you choose surveillance.

stem: A Male patient has carotid artery stenosis 48% high-risk, old age, multiple comorbidities dyslipidemia and HTN, slurred speech. What is the next step in management for this patient?
why_right: With 48% stenosis, even with symptoms (slurred speech), the degree of narrowing is below the 50% level at which revascularization offers benefit, and this patient is high-risk, elderly with multiple comorbidities, making procedural risk outweigh any gain. The keyed 'observation' means no intervention on the artery: best medical therapy (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP control) with follow-up imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. Carotid stenting is an alternative to endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis (≥50%, mainly 70 to 99%) in patients at high surgical risk; at 48% there is no indication for revascularization.
C. Endarterectomy benefits symptomatic patients with 70 to 99% stenosis (and selected 50 to 69%), ideally soon after the event; below 50% it gives no benefit and adds operative stroke risk.
key_concept:
Symptomatic carotid stenosis: degree of stenosis decides.
  • 70 to 99%: carotid endarterectomy, early after the event
  • 50 to 69%: consider endarterectomy in selected patients
  • <50%: best medical therapy only
  • Stenting: alternative when surgical risk is high and stenosis is significant
  • Near-total occlusion/complete occlusion: no surgery
exam_pearl: 'Observation' in carotid questions still means antiplatelet + statin + risk factor control, never doing nothing after a neurological symptom.

stem: 21-year-women presented to Emergency Room with right lower quadrant pain and anorexia. RLQ tenderness and rebound tenderness, WBC high. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: right lower quadrant pain and anorexia
why_right: The picture (RLQ pain, anorexia, rebound tenderness, high WBC) suggests appendicitis, but this is a 21-year-old woman, in whom gynecological causes (ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, ectopic pregnancy, PID) commonly mimic it. The key chooses CT abdomen, the most sensitive test, to confirm the diagnosis and exclude complications or alternatives before operating. A pregnancy test should precede any CT in a woman of reproductive age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Proceeding straight to surgery is reasonable only when the diagnosis is clear (e.g. a young man with classic findings), and the preferred approach today is laparoscopic, not open; in a young woman the diagnosis should be confirmed first.
C. Peritoneal signs (rebound tenderness) with leukocytosis can never be discharged; discharge fits only when examination and labs are reassuring.
key_concept:
Suspected appendicitis: choose imaging by patient group.
  • Adults, obese patients: CT abdomen (best sensitivity)
  • Children and pregnant women: ultrasound first, MRI if equivocal in pregnancy
  • Woman of reproductive age: β-hCG first, gynecological causes in the differential
  • Clear clinical diagnosis: appendectomy (laparoscopic preferred)
  • Abscess: drainage + antibiotics; phlegmon: antibiotics, conservative
exam_pearl: Young woman with RLQ pain: confirm before cutting; if she is pregnant, the imaging switches from CT to ultrasound/MRI.

stem: pregnant lady with RLQ pain vomiting, tenderness and leukocytosis, appropriate treatment
OptA: CT Abdomen and US (In one option)
key_concept:
Appendicitis in pregnancy: confirm with radiation-sparing imaging, then antibiotics plus appendectomy.
  • Imaging: US first in pregnant women and children; MRI if US inconclusive
  • CT: best sensitivity in non-pregnant adults; any age for abscess or phlegmon
  • Uncomplicated: empirical antibiotics + laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Phlegmon: IV antibiotics (conservative)
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "confirm/diagnose" points to imaging (US first in pregnancy), "treatment" points to antibiotics with appendectomy, never discharge.

stem: old patient underwent laparotomy 4 days ago and post-operatively developed absent bowel sounds, abdominal distension and can't pass stool, no fever or high Wbc. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Laparotomy "4 days ago" followed by "absent bowel sounds", distension and failure to pass stool, with "no fever or high WBC", is postoperative paralytic ileus. Ileus is managed conservatively, and the initial step is bowel rest with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids (with electrolyte correction). Most cases settle without intervention.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laxatives add load to a bowel that is not moving and are not used in ileus; early ambulation helps but is supportive only. Laxatives fit simple constipation with a working bowel.
C. Laparotomy is for peritonitis, strangulation or failure of conservative management; here there is no fever, no leukocytosis and no peritoneal signs.
key_concept:
Early postoperative ileus = conservative care first.
  • Surgery days ago: paralytic ileus or Ogilvie; surgery years ago: adhesive obstruction
  • Ileus: dilated small and large bowel, no transition point
  • Conservative: NPO, NGT decompression, IV fluids, correct electrolytes
  • Prolonged ileus: check potassium (hypokalemia causes ileus)
  • Operate only for peritonitis, strangulation or failed conservative care
exam_pearl: If "check serum potassium/electrolytes" is offered as the next step for prolonged ileus, that is the keyed choice in similar questions.

stem: 60 Y/O female, had large amount of Maroon-colored stool, she is pale and tachycardic, continued to bleed despite good resuscitation, abdomen is lax and soft and non tender, what is the initial management?
highlight_terms_source: continued to bleed despite good resuscitation
why_right: This recall's key is NGT because the lead-in asks for the initial management of "large amount of maroon-colored stool" with tachycardia and ongoing bleeding. Brisk upper GI bleeding can present as maroon or bright red stool, so the classic first step is to exclude an upper source with nasogastric aspiration before committing to a lower GI work-up. A bilious aspirate without blood makes an upper source less likely.
why_wrong_block:
B. Angiography localizes and embolizes active bleeding in a patient still bleeding despite resuscitation; it is the definitive next step after an upper source is excluded, which the twin recall keys for "most appropriate" management.
C. Colonoscopy suits a stable patient who can tolerate bowel preparation; massive ongoing bleeding in an unstable patient limits views and safety.
D. Barium enema has no role in acute bleeding: it cannot treat, rarely localizes active bleeding and obscures later angiography or endoscopy.
key_concept:
Massive hematochezia: resuscitate, exclude an upper source, then localize and treat.
  • Maroon or red stool + instability: think brisk upper GI bleed too
  • Exclude upper source: NG aspirate (classic) or upper endoscopy
  • Unstable or ongoing bleeding: CT angiography, then catheter angiography with embolization
  • Stable, tolerating prep: colonoscopy
  • No source: tagged RBC scan and small bowel evaluation
exam_pearl: Same scenario, two keys: "initial" = NGT (rule out upper source), "most appropriate" = angiography.

stem: 60 Y/O female, had large amount of Maroon-colored stool, she is pale and tachycardic, continued to bleed despite good resuscitation, abdomen is lax and soft and non tender, what is the Most Appropriate Management?
highlight_terms_source: continued to bleed despite good resuscitation
why_right: A 60-year-old with "large amount of maroon-colored stool", pale and tachycardic, who "continued to bleed despite good resuscitation" has ongoing hemodynamically significant lower GI bleeding. For the most appropriate management, angiography (CT angiography, then catheter angiography) localizes the active bleeding point and allows embolization without bowel preparation. The soft, non-tender abdomen argues against ischemia or peritonitis needing surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. NGT aspiration is the classic initial step to exclude an upper source of maroon stool (keyed in the twin "initial" recall), but it does not stop or localize lower GI bleeding.
C. Colonoscopy is first for a stable patient able to tolerate bowel preparation; with ongoing massive bleeding and instability, angiography is preferred.
D. Barium enema is never used in acute bleeding: it neither treats nor reliably localizes bleeding and interferes with later angiography or endoscopy.
key_concept:
Acute LGIB: stability decides the route.
  • Unstable: stabilize (large-bore IV, blood products, reverse anticoagulation) then CT angiography
  • Stable + can take prep + low suspicion of active bleeding: colonoscopy
  • Source found: hemostasis (endoscopic or embolization)
  • No source: colonoscopy if not done, then tagged RBC scan and small bowel evaluation
  • Surgery: failure of these or peritonitis
exam_pearl: "Initial" in the twin recall flips the key to NGT; "most appropriate" with ongoing bleeding means angiography.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0482 → A. NGT. Confirm before the exam.

stem: Old women presented with lower gi bleeding; on examination diffusely tender abdomen, pr exam showing fresh blood, patient is unstable despite receiving blood (BP Was Not Mentioned, Just Unstable). What is the most appropriate Next Step In Management:
key_concept:
LGIB next step depends on stability and peritoneal signs.
  • Unstable: resuscitate, then CT angiography and embolization
  • Stable + tolerates prep: colonoscopy
  • Peritonitis, ischemia or failed angiography: laparotomy
  • Coagulopathy: correct (FFP, reversal) alongside, not instead of, source control
  • No source found: tagged RBC scan, small bowel evaluation
exam_pearl: A soft non-tender abdomen with ongoing bleeding pushes to angiography; a diffusely tender abdomen raises ischemia or peritonitis and pushes toward surgery.

stem: Female pt came with epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting. O/E tenderness of the epigastric region. (It was very short Q no other predisposing factors or S&S) Amylase was high No other labs were mentioned. What will predict the severity of her case (something like that)
why_right: Epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting with epigastric tenderness and "amylase was high" is acute pancreatitis. The question asks what will predict severity: CRP is the standard single biochemical marker of severity, with a markedly raised level at about 48 hours indicating severe disease. It is cheap, widely available and reliable once enough time has passed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Procalcitonin rises earlier and is used to suggest infected necrosis or as an early marker within the first day; for a general severity question without timing, CRP is the keyed marker.
B. A raised ALT points to a gallstone (biliary) cause of pancreatitis; it identifies the etiology, not the severity.
D. ESR is a slow, nonspecific inflammatory marker with no role in grading acute pancreatitis.
key_concept:
Pancreatitis: diagnose with 2 of 3, grade severity separately.
  • Diagnosis: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥3× ULN, typical imaging
  • Severity marker: CRP (best at about 48 hours)
  • Scores: Ranson, Glasgow, APACHE II, BISAP
  • Raised ALT: suggests biliary cause
  • Procalcitonin: early marker, infected necrosis
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a short duration (hours, under a day), the related recall keys procalcitonin because CRP has not yet risen.

stem: Female pt came with epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting. O/E tenderness of the epigastric region. (It was very short Q no other predisposing factors or S&S) Amylase was high No other labs were mentioned. What will predict the severity of her case (something like that)
key_concept:
Severity marker in acute pancreatitis: time decides.
  • Under about 24 hours: procalcitonin (rises early)
  • Beyond a day or no timing: CRP (best at about 48 hours)
  • AST/ALT: etiology (biliary) or score components, not standalone severity
  • Scores: Ranson, Glasgow, APACHE II, BISAP
