stem: Mild swelling and redness with increased pain and tenderness at the site of surgical wound
why_right: Swelling, redness, "increased pain and tenderness" at the surgical wound is a surgical site infection or early wound collection. The source treatment is to open and explore the wound (remove sutures, drain pus, irrigate and pack), because pus is not cured by antibiotics. Here "surgical exploration" means exploring the wound, not reopening the abdomen.
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharge ignores an active wound infection; it fits only a clean healing wound or a resolved problem.
C. IV antibiotics are adjuncts when there is spreading cellulitis or systemic signs; alone they do not drain a collection in the wound.
D. Observation with culture delays drainage; a culture is taken when the wound is opened, not instead of opening it.
key_concept:
Postoperative wound problems: identify the collection, then drain.
  • SSI: open the wound, CT if deep infection suspected, image-guided drainage
  • Wound abscess: incision and drainage (wound exploration)
  • Seroma: painless, afebrile; explore, irrigate, leave open, dress
  • Intra-abdominal collection: small = antibiotics; ≥4×4 cm = percutaneous drainage
  • Unstable or generalized peritonitis: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Pus or a tender inflamed wound = open it; antibiotics alone are the trap.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option A printed as 'Surgical' at end of stem and 'exploration' (highlighted) as option A.

stem: 50 years old male patient K/C of DM. He did open abdominal surgery. In the 3rd post-operative days, he develop redness and swelling at the surgical site maybe tender swelling. Vitally stable (I think they mentioned no fever). What is the best management?
highlight_terms_source: redness and swelling at the surgical site
why_right: A diabetic on postoperative day 3 after open abdominal surgery with "redness and swelling at the surgical site" and tenderness has a surgical site infection. The source answer is to open and surgically debride the wound, draining any collection and removing nonviable tissue; diabetes raises the risk of a deeper or necrotizing process, so early source control is favoured over antibiotics alone. Stable vitals mean this is done at the wound, not by re-laparotomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Empiric IV antibiotics fit cellulitis without a collection or are added for systemic signs; on their own they do not drain an infected wound.
C. Culture and observation delays source control in a diabetic with an inflamed wound; culture is taken when the wound is opened.
key_concept:
Wound infection after surgery: source control first.
  • Days 4 to 5: classic timing of surgical site infection
  • SSI: open the wound, drain, debride, pack
  • Diabetes or immunosuppression: lower threshold, think necrotizing infection
  • Antibiotics: adjunct for cellulitis or systemic signs
  • Peritonitis or instability: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Crepitus, rapidly spreading redness or pain out of proportion signals necrotizing infection: urgent radical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.

stem: 50 years old male patient K/C of DM. He did open abdominal surgery. In the 3rd postoperative days, he develop redness and swelling at the surgical site maybe tender swelling. Vitally stable (I think they mentioned no fever). What is the best management?
highlight_terms_source: redness and swelling at the surgical site
why_right: Same scenario as the debridement variant: a diabetic on postoperative day 3 with "redness and swelling at the surgical site" and tenderness has a surgical site infection. The keyed answer is re-exploration of the wound: open it, drain any pus and debride, since an infected collection needs source control. The patient is "vitally stable", so this refers to the wound, not re-opening the abdomen.
why_wrong_block:
B. Empiric IV antibiotics alone fit cellulitis without a collection or are added for systemic signs; they do not drain the wound.
C. Culture and observation delays treatment; the culture is taken when the wound is opened.
key_concept:
Postoperative wound infection: open the wound.
  • SSI: open, drain, irrigate, pack; CT if deep infection suspected
  • Wound abscess: incision and drainage (wound exploration)
  • Seroma: painless and afebrile; explore, irrigate, leave open
  • Re-laparotomy: generalized peritonitis, anastomotic leak, instability
exam_pearl: "Re-exploration" for a stable patient with a red, swollen wound means the wound; peritonitis or instability would be needed to justify re-laparotomy.

stem: A 55-year-old female in ICU known case of diverticulitis underwent hartman procedure, 2nd-day post-surgery patient developed a decrease in urine output to 20 ml/hr, and central venous pressure was 10 with lower limb edema. Other examinations were unremarkable, all vitals were stable, and normal blood pressure. What is the appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: decrease in urine output to 20 ml/hr
why_right: This recall's key is re-exploration because the picture is read as a surgical cause after a Hartmann procedure: oliguria ("20 ml/hr") with a CVP that is NOT low ("CVP 10") and new "lower limb edema" means the patient is not simply dry, so a fluid problem is unlikely. The keyed reasoning is that raised intra-abdominal pressure (abdominal compartment syndrome compressing renal veins and the IVC) or an intra-abdominal surgical complication is the cause, and both are dealt with by returning to theatre.
why_wrong_block:
B. Renal duplex looks at renal artery and vein flow (renal artery stenosis or thrombosis, transplant kidney). Nothing here points to a primary renovascular event.
C. Abdominal US can show a collection or hydronephrosis, but views are poor on day 2 after a laparotomy with gas, dressings and a stoma; it is the choice when a stable patient needs a quick bedside look for a collection.
D. CT with contrast is the test for a stable patient with suspected abscess or leak (e.g. spiking fever after Hartmann). Here the kidneys are already failing to make urine, and IV contrast adds nephrotoxic risk.
key_concept:
Post-op oliguria: decide volume status before anything else.
  • Low CVP, tachycardia: hypovolemia, give a fluid challenge
  • Normal or high CVP, oliguria, edema: not a fluid problem, look for a surgical or renal cause
  • Oliguria + rising CVP + tense abdomen or high airway pressure: think abdominal compartment syndrome (bladder pressure, decompressive laparotomy)
  • Fever + tachycardia, stable: CT abdomen for collection
  • Always exclude a blocked urinary catheter first
exam_pearl: Low urine output with a LOW CVP is fluids; with a normal or high CVP and edema, stop giving fluid and look for a surgical cause.

stem: 60 yr old male underwent appendectomy, he presented 6 days post open appendectomy with red, swollen and tender wound site. What's the most appropriate (next step or management) ?
highlight_terms_source: red, swollen and tender wound site
why_right: A "red, swollen and tender wound" on day 6 after an OPEN appendectomy is a surgical site (wound) infection; days 5 to 7 is the classic window. The first step is to open the wound (remove sutures or staples) so pus can drain, then pack and dress it. If deep infection is still suspected after opening, imaging follows.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT abdomen is the step after the wound is opened, or first-line if there are signs of a deep or intra-abdominal collection (spiking fever, ileus, tenderness away from the wound). The findings here are confined to the wound.
C. US abdomen is used to look for a pelvic or subphrenic collection; a superficial wound infection is a clinical diagnosis and needs no imaging before drainage.
D. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus trapped under a closed wound. They are added when there is spreading cellulitis or systemic sepsis, not used instead of opening the wound.
key_concept:
Post-op infection ladder:
  • Superficial SSI (red, swollen, tender wound): open the wound
  • Wound abscess with pus: incision and drainage
  • Seroma: painless swelling, no fever, explore, irrigate, leave open, dress
  • Small intra-abdominal collection: antibiotics
  • Larger collection: percutaneous drainage under imaging
  • Unstable or generalized peritonitis: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Wound findings only (red, swollen, tender) means open the wound; peritonitis or feculent discharge flips it to laparotomy.

stem: Female patient a case of colon cancer came for colectomy, she lost 10% of her weight in the last few months, she have poor appetite, dietitian discovered she had low protein and caloric intake What is the best action?
why_right: She can eat and her gut works; the problem found by the dietitian is "low protein and caloric intake" with poor appetite. The least invasive route that fixes this is to increase oral protein and calorie intake (oral nutritional supplements) before the colectomy. Feeding route escalates only if the oral route fails or the gut cannot be used.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fluid restriction does nothing for malnutrition; it is used for fluid overload states such as heart failure, SIADH or advanced kidney disease.
C. TPN is for a non-functioning gut (obstruction, ileus, high-output fistula, short bowel). A functioning gut should be used, and TPN in a malnourished patient adds line sepsis and refeeding risk.
D. NG feeding is for a patient who cannot or will not take enough by mouth (coma, unsafe swallow, failed oral supplements). This patient can still eat, so oral supplementation comes first.
key_concept:
Nutrition route: if the gut works, use it, least invasive first.
  • Can eat: oral diet plus oral protein and calorie supplements
  • Cannot eat, short term (<1 month): nasogastric tube
  • Short term with aspiration risk: nasojejunal tube
  • Long term (>1 month): gastrostomy, or jejunostomy if aspiration risk
  • Non-functioning gut: parenteral nutrition
  • Watch for refeeding syndrome (low K, Mg, phosphate) in the malnourished
exam_pearl: "Can eat but eats too little" means supplement orally; tubes and TPN need a reason the mouth or gut cannot be used.

stem: Right Femur Fracture With Deformity, No Scar (Not Open), No Bleeding. What Is The Initial Management?
why_right: Even with no wound and "no bleeding" visible, a deformed femur fracture bleeds into the thigh, and a closed femoral shaft fracture can hide a large volume of blood. Following ABC, circulation comes first, so the initial priority is to control bleeding (resuscitate, then reduce and splint the limb, e.g. traction splint, which also limits ongoing loss).
why_wrong_block:
A. Limiting soft tissue damage matters (splinting does this too) but it is not life-threatening; it ranks after hemorrhage control.
C. Preserving joint movement and function is the goal of definitive fixation and rehabilitation, not the first priority.
D. Analgesia is given early and is important, but untreated hidden blood loss can kill; pain control comes after circulation is secured.
key_concept:
Long bone fracture priorities follow ATLS:
  • Airway, Breathing, then Circulation (stop bleeding, resuscitate)
  • Closed femur fracture: hidden blood loss into the thigh, watch for shock
  • Reduce and splint: lowers bleeding, pain and soft tissue injury
  • Then analgesia, neurovascular check, imaging
  • Definitive fixation and function last
exam_pearl: "No bleeding" means no visible bleeding; a femur fracture still bleeds internally, so hemorrhage control stays first.

stem: young Builder with reducable inguinal hernia reach scrotal asymptotic but concern about it
why_right: An adult ("young builder") with a primary, unilateral, reducible inguinal hernia that already "reaches the scrotum" and worries him should be repaired, and the standard adult operation is a tension-free mesh repair (open Lichtenstein). Mesh gives the lowest recurrence rate, which matters in a manual worker who strains heavily.
why_wrong_block:
A. Herniotomy (sac ligation alone) is the operation for children, whose problem is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall. Adults need the posterior wall reinforced.
C. Herniorrhaphy (suture or tissue repair without mesh) has a higher recurrence rate than mesh; it is kept for contaminated fields such as a strangulated hernia with bowel resection.
D. Watchful waiting suits an older or high-risk man with a small, minimally symptomatic hernia. A large inguinoscrotal hernia in a young labourer who wants it treated should be repaired.
key_concept:
Groin hernia operation choice:
  • Child: herniotomy
  • Adult, primary unilateral: open tension-free mesh repair
  • Bilateral, recurrent after open repair, or needs fast return to work: laparoscopic mesh repair
  • Femoral hernia: always repair (strangulation risk)
  • Strangulated or contaminated field: open repair, tissue repair if bowel resected
exam_pearl: Age decides the operation: child means herniotomy, adult means mesh; bilateral or recurrent pushes it to laparoscopic mesh.

stem: 68 years old presents to ER with bright red bleedy stool and he is known case of hypertension and colorectal polyps. He is pale and tachycardia Bp 160/90, 110 bpm Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management:
why_right: The lead-in asks for the INITIAL management. He is "pale" with "HR 110": he is losing blood and compensating. The BP of 160/90 is falsely reassuring in a known hypertensive, because his usual pressure is likely higher, so a 'normal-looking' BP can already be a relative drop. Resuscitation with large-bore IV access, IV fluid and blood comes before any test.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is done after resuscitation and bowel preparation, usually in a stable patient. It is the main test in a stable lower GI bleed, but not the first step in a tachycardic patient.
C. A plain abdominal CT does not locate active bleeding. When imaging is needed for active lower GI bleeding, CT angiography is used, and only after resuscitation has started.
key_concept:
Acute lower GI bleed algorithm:
  • Step 1 always: assess and resuscitate (2 large-bore IVs, fluids, blood, reverse anticoagulation)
  • Unstable or brisk ongoing bleed: CT angiography, then embolization or endoscopic therapy
  • Stable: colonoscopy after bowel prep
  • Source still not found: tagged RBC scan, small bowel work-up
  • Exclude an upper GI source in brisk bleeding with shock
exam_pearl: "Initial" in any bleeding patient means resuscitate; read tachycardia and pallor, not the BP, in a hypertensive.

stem: 68 years old presents to ER with bright red bleedy stool and he is known case of hypertension and colorectal polyps. He is pale and tachycardia Bp 160/90 HR 110 bpm Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is CT angiography because the lead-in asks for the most appropriate MANAGEMENT (not the initial step, which is the sister recall). In a pale, tachycardic patient with active bright red rectal bleeding, the algorithm is resuscitate and then do CT angiography, which shows where the bleeding is coming from and guides embolization or targeted endoscopy. The source chose the step that finds and treats the bleeding over supportive care.
why_wrong_block:
A. The option text was not recalled, so it cannot be assessed; the compiler notes that urgent colonoscopy was NOT among this recall's options. Colonoscopy would in any case suit a stable patient after bowel prep, not one who is pale and tachycardic.
B. IV fluid and blood is the INITIAL step and is always started first, but it supports the patient rather than finding or stopping the bleed. It is the answer when the question asks "initial" or "first".
key_concept:
Same patient, different lead-in:
  • "Initial" or "first": IV fluid and blood
  • "Most appropriate management" in an actively bleeding, tachycardic patient: CT angiography (after resuscitation)
  • Stable patient: colonoscopy after bowel prep
  • Plain CT abdomen does not locate bleeding; it needs the arterial (angio) phase. Another recall of this card wrote the option as "CT with contrast"
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "initial" keys resuscitation; "most appropriate" keys the step that localizes the bleed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No Urgent Colonoscopy option. Another recall: same options but it came as CT with contrast, not angio.

stem: 68 years old presents to ER with bright red bleedy stool and he is known case of hypertension and colorectal polyps. He is pale and tachycardia Bp 160/90 HR 110 bpm Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
key_concept:
How to decide:
  • "Initial" + tachycardia or pallor: IV fluid and blood
  • Active bleed, still unstable or brisk, after resuscitation: CT angiography
  • Stable, bleeding settled: colonoscopy after bowel prep
  • A sister recall of this stem is keyed to IV fluid and blood for "initial"; one without a colonoscopy option is keyed to CT angiography
exam_pearl: Tachycardia and pallor outweigh a normal or high BP in a hypertensive; then let the lead-in verb and the patient's stability choose between resuscitation, CT angiography and colonoscopy.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient was diagnosed with a perforated peptic ulcer and underwent surgical repair with an omental patch. What is the most appropriate Preventive Measure?
why_right: After an omental patch repair, prevention means removing the causes of the ulcer. NSAIDs (including aspirin) are one of the two main causes of peptic ulcer and perforation, and stopping them directly lowers the risk of recurrence and re-perforation. Of the two options listed, only avoiding NSAIDs targets a cause.
why_wrong_block: A. A healthy diet is general advice; diet does not cause or prevent peptic ulcer, so it does not prevent recurrence.
key_concept:
After perforated PU repair, treat the cause:
  • Stop NSAIDs and aspirin (or protect with a PPI if they are essential)
  • Test for and eradicate H. pylori
  • PPI therapy to heal the ulcer
  • Stop smoking
  • Diet changes do not prevent recurrence
exam_pearl: If the options include H. pylori testing or eradication, that is often keyed over avoiding NSAIDs unless the stem names an NSAID user (see the sister recall).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): elderly patient, perforated duodenal ulcer surgically repaired and appropriately treated; most important preventive measure? A. Stop NSAIDs (highlighted), B. Diet with high fiber, C. Regular follow-up for gastric health.

stem: Patient was diagnosed with a perforated peptic ulcer and underwent surgical repair with an omental patch. What is the most appropriate advice to give this patient after surgery?
why_right: H. pylori is the commonest cause of peptic ulcer, and the stem gives no NSAID history. After an omental patch, which only closes the hole, the most important advice is to test for H. pylori and eradicate it if positive, because eradication markedly reduces recurrence and re-perforation. Patch repair is routinely followed by H. pylori eradication and a PPI.
why_wrong_block:
A. A healthy diet is reasonable general advice but does not cause or prevent peptic ulcer, so it does not reduce recurrence.
B. Avoiding NSAIDs is correct advice and is the answer when the stem names NSAID or aspirin use (or when H. pylori testing is not offered). Here no NSAID use is mentioned, so the commonest cause, H. pylori, takes priority.
key_concept:
Peptic ulcer causes and how to prevent recurrence:
  • H. pylori: test (urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy), then eradicate
  • Classic first line: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin; bismuth quadruple if it fails (newer guidance prefers bismuth quadruple first where clarithromycin resistance is high)
  • Confirm eradication with a urea breath test
  • Before a breath test, stop the PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks (avoids false negatives)
  • NSAIDs: stop, or add a PPI if they are essential
exam_pearl: No NSAID in the stem means H. pylori; a stated NSAID or aspirin user with only diet versus NSAIDs offered means avoid NSAIDs.

stem: Patient was diagnosed with a perforated peptic ulcer and underwent surgical repair with an omental patch. What is the most appropriate advice to give this patient after surgery?
why_right: After a perforated ulcer is closed with an omental (Graham) patch, the operation only fixes the hole; the ulcer and its cause remain. Most perforated duodenal ulcers are driven by H. pylori, so the key postoperative step is to test for it and give eradication therapy (PPI plus antibiotics), which markedly reduces ulcer recurrence and re-perforation. That is why "Abx for Pylori" is the most appropriate advice here.
why_wrong_block:
A. A healthy diet is generic advice; diet does not cause or heal peptic ulcers and does nothing to prevent recurrence after a perforation.
B. Avoiding NSAIDs is sensible and is the key step when the stem stresses NSAID use, but the stem gives no NSAID history; the recall keys eradication of the commonest cause, H. pylori.
key_concept:
Perforated peptic ulcer: repair the hole, then treat the cause.
  • Perforated duodenal ulcer: omental (Graham) patch closure
  • Perforated antral gastric ulcer: partial distal gastrectomy
  • After repair: PPI plus H. pylori eradication (first line PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin)
  • Confirm eradication with urea breath test
  • NSAID user: stop NSAIDs
exam_pearl: If the stem highlights chronic NSAID use for joint pain, "stop NSAIDs" becomes the targeted advice; otherwise eradicate H. pylori.

stem: Female patient a case of colon cancer came for colectomy, she lost 10% of her weight in the last few months, she have poor appetite, dietitian discovered she had low protein and caloric intake What is the best action?
why_right: This patient is malnourished before major surgery (10% weight loss, low protein and calorie intake) but her gut works and she can still eat by mouth. The first step in nutrition is to check gut function, and the least invasive route that works is preferred, so oral protein and energy supplements are the best action to optimise her before colectomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Restricting fluid has no role in correcting malnutrition; it is used for fluid overload states such as heart or renal failure, not here.
C. TPN is for a non functioning gut (obstruction, ileus, short bowel) or when enteral feeding fails; it carries line sepsis and refeeding risks and is not needed when she can eat.
D. NG tube feeding is for a functioning gut when the patient cannot or will not eat enough by mouth (coma, dysphagia, unsafe swallow); she can still take oral supplements.
key_concept:
Nutrition route ladder: use the gut if it works, and the least invasive route first.
  • Can eat: oral supplements
  • Functioning gut, cannot eat, acute (<1 month): NG tube; aspiration risk: NJ tube
  • Chronic (>1 month): gastrostomy; aspiration risk: jejunostomy
  • Non functioning gut: parenteral nutrition
  • Severely malnourished: watch for refeeding (low K, Mg, PO4)
exam_pearl: Poor appetite with a working gut still means oral first; jump to tube or TPN only if oral intake fails or the gut does not work.

stem: 28yo female came ER with right lower quadrant pain for 12h, physical Examination revealed suprapubic and lower quadrant tenderness without rebound Wbc 12.5 US: inconclusive What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A young woman with RLQ pain plus "suprapubic" tenderness, no rebound, a mild WBC of 12.5 and an "inconclusive" (transabdominal) US has a differential that includes gynaecological causes (ovarian cyst, torsion, ectopic, PID). The recall's key is transvaginal US because it images the ovaries, adnexa and pelvis far better than transabdominal US, avoids radiation in a woman of reproductive age, and can identify or exclude a pelvic cause before moving to CT.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT has the best sensitivity for appendicitis and is the usual next step in a non pregnant adult (especially obese) when US is inconclusive; the recall prefers to finish the radiation free pelvic assessment first.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy is invasive; it is for a persistently unclear picture after imaging or a clinically deteriorating patient, not for a stable patient with mild findings.
D. Open appendectomy needs a confident diagnosis of appendicitis (migrating pain, McBurney rebound, imaging support); here there is no rebound and imaging is inconclusive.
key_concept:
RLQ pain in a woman of reproductive age: always exclude pregnancy and pelvic pathology.
  • First: pregnancy test
  • Children and pregnant women: US first (MRI if pregnant and US inconclusive)
  • Non pregnant adult, inconclusive US: CT abdomen has best sensitivity
  • Suspected ovarian or adnexal cause: transvaginal US
  • Clear appendicitis: appendectomy
exam_pearl: "Suprapubic tenderness" in a young woman pushes toward a pelvic cause and TVUS; an obese adult with classic RIF signs and inconclusive US goes to CT.

stem: Pt after splenectomy surgery presented with multiple episodes of intestinal obstruction. Now complaining of abdominal distension, pain, rigidity, sluggish bowel sounds. Vitals stable. X ray air fluid level. What is the initial management?
why_right: Previous abdominal surgery (splenectomy) with "multiple episodes" of obstruction and air fluid levels on X ray means recurrent adhesive small bowel obstruction. An uncomplicated, soft abdomen would get NGT, fluids and bowel rest, but here the abdomen is "rigid", which signals peritonitis (possible strangulation or perforation). The recall's key is exploratory laparotomy because peritonitis is an absolute indication for surgery, so stable vitals do not change the decision.
why_wrong_block:
A. Paracentesis is for ascites (diagnostic or therapeutic), not for mechanical bowel obstruction with peritonism.
B. Gastrografin is a water soluble contrast study used in uncomplicated adhesive SBO to predict and help resolution; it is contraindicated once there are signs of peritonitis or strangulation.
D. NGT, analgesia and bowel rest is the correct first approach for uncomplicated SBO (soft abdomen, no peritonism); rigidity and recurrent episodes take this patient beyond conservative care.
key_concept:
Bowel obstruction: conservative first unless there is a surgical indication.
  • Uncomplicated: fluids, electrolytes, NG decompression, nil by mouth
  • Imaging: X ray first, CT confirms
  • Laparotomy if peritonitis (rigidity, rebound)
  • Laparotomy if strangulation (fever, tachycardia, constant pain, mesenteric stranding on CT)
  • Laparotomy if conservative management fails
  • Surgery years ago: adhesions; days ago: paralytic ileus
exam_pearl: The word "rigidity" turns a drip and suck SBO into an operative case even with normal vitals.

stem: Case for patient with PUD present with guarding and rigidity and rebound tenderness (perforation) What is the *initial* next step?
why_right: Guarding, rigidity and rebound in a PUD patient mean perforation with generalised peritonitis, which causes major third space fluid loss and early sepsis. The lead in asks for the "initial" step: resuscitate first (IV access, crystalloid fluids, with NPO, NG tube, PPI and antibiotics alongside), then take the patient to theatre once optimised.
why_wrong_block: B. Exploratory laparotomy with patch repair is the definitive treatment, but taking an under resuscitated, peritonitic patient straight to theatre is unsafe; it is the answer when the question asks for definitive or most appropriate management.
key_concept:
Perforated peptic ulcer sequence:
  • 1. ABC and IV fluid resuscitation (initial)
  • 2. NPO, NG tube, IV PPI, broad spectrum antibiotics, analgesia
  • 3. Erect chest X ray: free air under diaphragm; CT if unclear
  • 4. Laparotomy: duodenal ulcer, omental (Graham) patch; antral gastric ulcer, partial gastrectomy
  • 5. H. pylori eradication after repair
exam_pearl: "Initial" step = fluids; "definitive" or "most appropriate management" = laparotomy and patch repair.

stem: A 3 years old came with unilateral undescended testis and no scrotum in the affected side what other conditions could be accompanied (something like this in surgery and medical part not pedi) Which of the following is associated Finding?
why_right: An undescended testis with an underdeveloped hemiscrotum on the "affected side" is cryptorchidism. The testis descends with the processus vaginalis, and in most undescended testes this processus stays patent, so an indirect inguinal hernia is the most common associated finding (usually repaired at the same time as orchidopexy).
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypospadias is associated with cryptorchidism too, but it is the association asked when the question focuses on sexual development or DSD; as a general associated finding the patent processus (hernia) is commoner.
C. Pyloric stenosis is a first born male infant problem with projectile non bilious vomiting at around 6 weeks; it has no link to testicular descent.
D. Congenital heart disease is not a typical association of isolated cryptorchidism; it suggests a syndrome (e.g. Noonan, Down) only when other features are given.
key_concept:
Undescended testis essentials:
  • Most common association: indirect inguinal hernia (patent processus vaginalis)
  • Genital association: hypospadias (if both, consider DSD workup)
  • Palpable testis: orchidopexy
  • Non palpable testis: diagnostic laparoscopy
  • Long term risks: infertility and testicular cancer
exam_pearl: Generic "associated finding" = inguinal hernia; "related to sexual development" = hypospadias.

stem: A 3 years old came with unilateral undescended testis and no scrotum in the affected side what other conditions could be accompanied (something like this in surgery and medical part not pedi) Which of the following is associated with this finding and related to sexual development?
why_right: The lead in narrows the question to an association "related to sexual development". Cryptorchidism and hypospadias are both disorders of male genital development that share androgen related causes, so they often coexist; hypospadias with an undescended testis should prompt evaluation for a disorder of sex development.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inguinal hernia is the most common associated finding overall (patent processus vaginalis), but it is a structural defect, not a disorder of sexual development.
C. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile non bilious vomiting in a young infant and is unrelated to genital development.
D. Congenital heart disease is not linked to sexual development and is only expected when a syndrome is described.
key_concept:
Cryptorchidism associations by lead in:
  • General associated finding: inguinal hernia
  • Related to sexual development: hypospadias
  • Hypospadias + undescended (especially non palpable) testis: evaluate for DSD (karyotype)
  • Cryptorchidism: most common disorder of sexual differentiation in boys
exam_pearl: Same stem, different lead in: "sexual development" flips the answer from hernia to hypospadias.

stem: A hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen finger after pulling the skin around the nail a few days ago. Nail bed is intact
highlight_terms_source: pulling the skin around the nail
why_right: Swelling of the finger a few days after "pulling the skin around the nail" (a hangnail) with an "intact" nail bed is acute paronychia: infection of the soft tissue fold around the nail, usually Staph aureus, after minor trauma to the cuticle. Occupations with repeated manipulation or wet work (hairdressers, cleaners) are typical.
why_wrong_block:
A. Felon is an abscess of the closed pulp space of the fingertip, with a tense, throbbing, very painful pad, usually after a puncture wound; here the problem is at the nail fold.
C. Onychomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the nail plate (thickened, discoloured, brittle nail) without acute swelling; here the nail is intact and the onset is acute.
D. Cellulitis is diffuse spreading redness of skin and subcutis, often with fever; the localised periungual swelling after a hangnail is more specifically paronychia.
key_concept:
Finger infections by site:
  • Nail fold (periungual): paronychia, after hangnail or nail biting; abscess needs incision and drainage
  • Chronic paronychia: wet work, often Candida
  • Pulp of fingertip: felon, urgent drainage
  • Nail plate: onychomycosis
  • Flexor sheath: Kanavel signs, flexor tenosynovitis
  • Diffuse skin redness: cellulitis
exam_pearl: Nail fold = paronychia; fingertip pulp = felon.

stem: A patient presents with a firm, painless, raised pink papule. Upon taking history the patient told you she had an old scar due to burn. What is the type of ulcer?
why_right: A new lesion arising in an "old scar due to burn" is Marjolin ulcer: malignant change, most often squamous cell carcinoma, in a chronic scar or non healing wound, typically many years after the injury. A firm, raised, painless lesion in a burn scar must be biopsied to confirm it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Arterial ulcers are painful, punched out ulcers on the toes or pressure points with absent pulses and ischaemic skin; they are not linked to burn scars.
B. Cushing ulcer is a stress peptic ulcer of the stomach or duodenum after head injury or raised intracranial pressure; it is not a skin lesion.
D. Neuropathic ulcers occur on pressure points of an insensate foot (diabetes, leprosy) and are painless but punched out with callus; they do not arise in burn scars.
key_concept:
Ulcer eponyms and types:
  • Marjolin: SCC in a chronic burn scar or non healing wound; treat with biopsy, then wide excision
  • Curling: stress gastric or duodenal ulcer after major burns
  • Cushing: stress ulcer after head injury or raised ICP
  • Arterial: painful, absent pulses
  • Venous: gaiter area, intact pulses, dark skin
  • Neuropathic: painless, pressure points, insensate foot
exam_pearl: Burns + skin lesion in the scar = Marjolin; burns + GI bleed = Curling ulcer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): 60-year-old woman with an erythematous, oozing, painful lesion on her left arm with history of burn injury on the same side; options Neuropathic / Ulcer / Marjolin; Marjolin highlighted.

stem: A child with a painless neck nodule that moves up and down, moves up with tongue protrusion. What is the most appropriate treatment ?
why_right: A painless midline neck nodule in a child that "moves up with tongue protrusion" is a thyroglossal duct cyst, a remnant of the thyroid's descent tract that is attached to the hyoid. Treatment is surgical excision by the Sistrunk procedure (cyst, tract and central part of the hyoid), which prevents recurrence and recurrent infection; ultrasound is done first to confirm a normal thyroid elsewhere.
why_wrong_block:
B. Needle aspiration only empties the cyst temporarily; the epithelial tract remains, so it recurs and can become infected. Aspiration is not definitive treatment.
C. Reassurance is wrong because thyroglossal cysts do not regress, tend to get infected, and rarely harbour carcinoma; they should be excised.
key_concept:
Pediatric neck masses:
  • Midline, moves with tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Sistrunk excision
  • Lateral, anterior to sternocleidomastoid: branchial cleft cyst; excision
  • Lateral, soft, transilluminates: cystic hygroma; sclerotherapy, then surgery
  • Moves with swallowing only: thyroid origin
  • Before excision: US to confirm a normal thyroid gland
exam_pearl: Excision must include the middle of the hyoid (Sistrunk); simple cyst excision recurs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: Pedia Pt with typical symptoms of thyroglossal cyst (not written). What is the management? A. Surgical excision. The fuller 'Possible Recall' is used as stem.

stem: A 60-year-old man complaining of right knee pain for several years that has increased over the last few months. He also has noticed frequent knee clicks. A diagnosis of osteoarthritis is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: A 60-year-old with years of knee pain, slowly worsening, with clicks (crepitus) has the classic picture of osteoarthritis. OA is a clinical diagnosis: in patients aged 45 or over with activity-related pain and little or no morning stiffness, no test is needed to confirm it. The lead-in asks how to confirm the diagnosis, not what baseline imaging to order.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bilateral knee X-rays: not needed to confirm OA, and X-ray changes correlate poorly with symptoms. Right when the stem asks for baseline imaging or there are atypical features (choose standing films).
B. MRI of the right knee: reserved for suspected internal derangement (meniscal or ligament injury with locking or giving way) or an unclear diagnosis.
D. Arthroscopy for the right knee: invasive and has no role in diagnosing OA; used only for selected mechanical problems.
key_concept:
OA is diagnosed clinically; imaging is for atypical cases or baseline.
  • Age ≥ 45 + activity-related pain + short (≤ 30 min) morning stiffness = clinical OA
  • 'Confirm the diagnosis' = no further investigation
  • 'Baseline/next imaging' = standing (weight-bearing) plain X-ray
  • X-ray: joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
exam_pearl: Read the verb: 'confirm suspected OA' means no test; 'next investigation' in OA means standing X-ray.

stem: 50 years old male patient K/C of DM . He did open abdominal surgery. In the 3rd post-operative days, he develop redness and swelling at the surgical site maybe tender swelling. Vitally stable (I think they mentioned no fever). What is the best management?
highlight_terms_source: redness and swelling at the surgical site
why_right: Redness and tender swelling at the incision on post-operative day 3 in a diabetic is read by this recall as a surgical site infection with infected or devitalized tissue in the wound. The source's reasoning is source control: open the wound, drain any pus and debride dead tissue, because antibiotics cannot penetrate a collection or necrotic tissue, and diabetes raises the risk of rapid deep spread. On that reading, surgical debridement is the best management.
why_wrong_block:
B. Empiric IV antibiotics are an adjunct (for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs or immunocompromise), not a substitute for opening and debriding an infected wound with a collection.
C. A wound swab is taken when the wound is opened, but observing an established infection in a diabetic delays source control and risks deep or necrotizing spread.
D. Reassurance fits a seroma (painless swelling without redness or fever); here the wound is red and tender, which is infection.
key_concept:
Post-operative wound problems: identify the collection, then drain it.
  • Superficial SSI: open the wound, drain, debride, dress
  • Wound abscess: incision and drainage
  • Seroma: painless swelling, no redness or fever
  • Small intra-abdominal collection: antibiotics
  • Large collection: percutaneous drainage under imaging
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Antibiotics treat cellulitis; pus or dead tissue in a wound needs a knife, not a drip.

stem: Patient presents after 30 minutes of slurred speech that resolved, no trauma or drug use or fever. Carotid shows stenosis 48% Best management besides controlling risk factors?
highlight_terms_source: 30 minutes of slurred speech that resolved
why_right: Thirty minutes of slurred speech that fully resolved is a TIA, and carotid imaging shows 48% stenosis, which is below the 50% level at which revascularization is considered for a symptomatic patient. Below that level there is no benefit from endarterectomy or stenting, so management is best medical therapy and observation: antiplatelet, statin and control of blood pressure, glucose and smoking.
why_wrong_block:
B. Carotid stenting is an alternative to endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis in patients at high surgical risk; it is not indicated for 48%.
C. Carotid thrombectomy is not a standard treatment for carotid stenosis; mechanical thrombectomy is for an acute large-vessel intracranial occlusion in a current stroke.
D. Endarterectomy is right for symptomatic stenosis of 70 to 99% (and selected 50 to 69%), ideally within 2 weeks of the TIA; 48% is below the threshold.
key_concept:
Symptomatic carotid stenosis: the percentage decides.
  • Under 50%: medical therapy only (antiplatelet, statin, risk factors)
  • 50 to 69%: endarterectomy in selected patients
  • 70 to 99%: endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks
  • Complete occlusion: no surgery
  • Initial imaging after TIA: carotid duplex
exam_pearl: Change the number to 70% or more and the answer flips to carotid endarterectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original typed recall: pt with HTN, dyslipidemia came with TIA for 30 minutes, Echo: carotid stenosis 48%; options Observe / Carotid endarterectomy / Carotid Stent; Observe highlighted.

stem: long scenario about an elderly who had colectomy, and post operation he had dehydration and increased skin turgor with postural hypotension. ABG results: PH 7.8 (high) HCO3 48 (high) PCO2 44 (high) PO2 (low) What is your interpretation?
why_right: The pH is high with a high HCO3 (48), so the primary disorder is metabolic alkalosis, from loss of gastric acid and volume after colectomy (dehydration, postural hypotension). Respiratory compensation would raise PCO2 well above normal (expected roughly 0.7 × HCO3 + 21, about 55); a PCO2 of 44 is essentially normal, so no meaningful compensation has occurred and the pH remains markedly raised. This recall's key is therefore uncompensated metabolic alkalosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. The word 'compensated' does not fit a pH this high, and neither disorder is compensating the other. Strictly, a PCO2 well below the expected value would mean a second, respiratory alkalosis, but exam keys read a normal PCO2 as no compensation.
C. Respiratory alkalosis is the primary problem only when PCO2 is low and HCO3 falls to compensate; here HCO3 is high and PCO2 is not low.
D. Respiratory compensation would show a clearly raised PCO2 near the expected value; a PCO2 of 44 is too close to normal to call compensation.
key_concept:
ABG reading in three steps.
  • pH: high = alkalosis, low = acidosis
  • Which value moves the same way as pH: HCO3 up with pH up = metabolic alkalosis
  • Compensation for metabolic alkalosis: PCO2 rises, expected about 0.7 × HCO3 + 21
  • PCO2 near normal = uncompensated
  • Vomiting or NG loss = HCl loss = hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
exam_pearl: Compare the actual PCO2 with the expected one: normal PCO2 with high HCO3 means no compensation yet.

stem: A previously healthy 55-year-old man undergoes elective right hemicolectomy for a stage I (T2N0M0) cancer of the cecum. His postoperative ileus is somewhat prolonged, and on the fifth postoperative day his nasogastric tube is still in place. Physical examination reveals diminished skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension. Pertinent laboratory values are as follows: What is the patient’s acid–base abnormality?
highlight_terms_source: nasogastric tube is still in place
diminished skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and orthostatic hypotension
why_right: Prolonged ileus with the nasogastric tube still in place on day 5 means continuous loss of gastric HCl, and the patient is volume depleted (poor skin turgor, dry mucosa, orthostatic hypotension). This produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis maintained by volume depletion. The lungs respond by hypoventilating, so PCO2 rises: metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. The laboratory values were not preserved in the recall, so the clinical setting is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Uncompensated means PCO2 stays normal; respiratory compensation develops within hours, so by day 5 some rise in PCO2 is expected.
B. Respiratory acidosis needs hypoventilation as the primary problem (for example COPD or sedation), with low pH; NG loss gives a high pH from a metabolic cause.
C. A combined metabolic and respiratory alkalosis would need a low PCO2 from a second cause such as pain, sepsis or anxiety driving hyperventilation; nothing here suggests that.
key_concept:
GI losses decide the acid-base disorder.
  • Vomiting or NG suction: HCl loss = metabolic alkalosis (low Cl, low K)
  • Diarrhea: HCO3 and K loss = hypokalemic metabolic acidosis
  • Compensation of metabolic alkalosis: hypoventilation, PCO2 rises
  • Treatment: normal saline plus potassium
  • Compensation cannot be confirmed without an ABG or VBG
exam_pearl: NG tube or vomiting = alkalosis; diarrhea = acidosis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Laboratory values not included in the recall.

stem: thyroid case TSH normal Ultrasound : 4×4 cm Besthesda classified = 0 FNA done but Inaccurate What the next?
why_right: With a normal TSH the nodule is not hot, so the pathway is ultrasound then FNA. The FNA was inadequate (Bethesda category 1, nondiagnostic), which gives no information on benign versus malignant. A nondiagnostic FNA is repeated, ideally under ultrasound guidance, before any decision on surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. A thyroid scan is used when TSH is low, to look for a hot autonomous nodule; with a normal TSH it does not replace cytology.
C. Total thyroidectomy is for confirmed malignancy (Bethesda 6) or other clear indications; operating without a cytological diagnosis is premature. Persistently nondiagnostic results on repeat FNA may then lead to diagnostic surgery.
key_concept:
Bethesda result drives the next step.
  • 1 Nondiagnostic: repeat FNA (US guided)
  • 2 Benign: ultrasound follow up
  • 3 Atypia of undetermined significance: repeat FNA
  • 4 Follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy
  • 5 Suspicious for malignancy: manage as 4 or 6
  • 6 Malignant: total (near total) thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Low TSH sends you to a scan; normal TSH with a failed FNA sends you back to FNA.

stem: A 32 years old female presented with severe pelvic pain and hypotension after MVA. CT: showed pelvic hematoma and active bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: pelvic pain and hypotension after MVA
why_right: After an MVA with severe pelvic pain, hypotension and a CT showing a pelvic hematoma with active bleeding, this is hemorrhagic shock from a pelvic (retroperitoneal) source. The priority is circulation: resuscitate with blood products (pRBCs, ideally balanced with plasma and platelets) and stabilize the pelvis with a binder, then control the bleeding by angioembolization or pelvic packing. Among the options, transfusion is the correct immediate management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laparotomy is for intraperitoneal bleeding (for example positive FAST with instability); opening the abdomen does not control retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding and can release tamponade.
C. Crystalloid and observation suit a stable patient without active bleeding; a hypotensive patient with active extravasation needs blood, and large volumes of crystalloid worsen coagulopathy.
key_concept:
Hypotensive pelvic fracture: resuscitate, stabilize, embolize.
  • Blood products (massive transfusion protocol if needed)
  • Pelvic binder to reduce pelvic volume
  • Active arterial extravasation on CT: angioembolization
  • Alternative: preperitoneal pelvic packing or external fixation
  • Positive FAST and unstable: laparotomy for the abdominal source
exam_pearl: Blood in the pelvis is not fixed by a laparotomy; blood in the peritoneum is.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): Female patient after MVA presented to the ED, hypotensive 90/50, CT showed pelvic hematoma and deep internal active bleed; options A. Blood transfusion (highlighted) / B. Ex. Lap.

stem: A patient presented to the ED after he was stabbed in his chest. Upon examination he had hypotension, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck veins. Lungs were clear bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A stab to the chest with hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins is Beck's triad, and clear lungs bilaterally rule out a pneumothorax or hemothorax as the cause. Blood in the pericardial sac compresses the heart and limits filling, so the diagnosis is cardiac tamponade. It is confirmed by FAST or echo and treated by pericardiocentesis or surgical decompression when unstable.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial contusion follows blunt trauma and presents with arrhythmias or a raised troponin, not muffled heart sounds after a stab wound.
B. Hemothorax causes hypotension with decreased breath sounds and dullness on one side, and the neck veins are usually flat from blood loss.
C. Tension pneumothorax also gives hypotension and raised JVP, but with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and tracheal shift; the lungs here are clear.
key_concept:
Hypotension plus distended neck veins after chest trauma: listen to the lungs.
  • Clear equal breath sounds + muffled heart = tamponade
  • Absent breath sounds + hyperresonance + tracheal shift = tension pneumothorax
  • Dull side + flat neck veins = massive hemothorax
  • Tamponade extras: pulsus paradoxus, low-voltage ECG
  • Unstable tamponade: pericardiocentesis
exam_pearl: Raised JVP with hypotension is tamponade or tension pneumothorax; breath sounds separate them.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): Patient with MVA came with muffled heart sound, BP 90/60. Diagnosis? A cardiac contusion / B. Pneumothorax / C. Cardiac tamponade / D. Heamothorax (no option marked).

stem: A 75 year old female K/C of Afib and recent unintentional weight loss, presented to the ER with severe abdominal pain that is described as out of proportion, on examination the abdomen was soft but tender with decreased bowel sound.
why_right: An elderly woman with atrial fibrillation (embolic source) and pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen is acute mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise; recent weight loss may reflect chronic intestinal ischemia (food fear). CT angiography is the test of choice: it is fast, shows the embolus or thrombus and the state of the bowel, and guides revascularization. It should not be delayed for other tests.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lactate supports ischemia but is nonspecific and may be normal early; a normal lactate does not exclude mesenteric ischemia.
B. Plain X-ray is usually normal early and only shows late signs (pneumatosis, free air); it is the first test for obstruction or perforation.
C. Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and cannot reliably assess the mesenteric vessels in an acute abdomen; it is the first test for biliary pain.
key_concept:
Acute mesenteric ischemia: suspect clinically, confirm with CT angiography.
  • Risk: AF, recent MI, valve disease, elderly with vascular disease
  • Hallmark: severe pain, benign abdomen
  • Late: bloody diarrhea, peritonitis, lactic acidosis
  • Test of choice: CT angiography
  • Treatment: heparin, revascularization, resect dead bowel
exam_pearl: AF plus pain out of proportion to examination = mesenteric ischemia = CT angiography.

stem: A patient with history of chronic intermittent claudication presented with sudden onset of acute limb ischemia. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
highlight_terms_source: sudden onset of acute limb ischemia
why_right: Sudden limb ischemia on a background of chronic claudication is acute-on-chronic ischemia, usually thrombosis on an atherosclerotic plaque. The lead-in asks for the initial diagnostic test: bedside Doppler ultrasound assesses arterial and venous signals, grades the threat to the limb and localizes the occlusion, and it is done after heparin is started. CT angiography follows as the confirmatory test if the limb is not immediately threatened.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT angiography is the confirmatory (most appropriate) test for planning revascularization, not the initial bedside test; with paralysis, imaging is skipped altogether.
C. ABI is the first test for chronic peripheral arterial disease (claudication), not for an acute ischemic limb, where Doppler signals guide urgency.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia ladder: heparin, Doppler, CT angiography.
  • 6 Ps: pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis
  • Initial test: Doppler ultrasound
  • Confirmatory: CT angiography
  • Paralysis or motor loss: skip imaging, go to theatre
  • Embolic (AF): embolectomy; thrombotic: catheter-directed thrombolysis or bypass
  • Chronic PAD: ABI first
exam_pearl: 'Initial' test = Doppler; 'most appropriate' or confirmatory test = CT angiography.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C present to the clinic for regular follow-up. His examination reveals a palpable right upper quadrant mass. CT scan of his abdomen shows a large 6*6 cm mass in the right lobe of the liver. A mass biopsy confirms the diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management steps at this stage?
why_right: A single 6 × 6 cm biopsy-proven HCC confined to the right lobe, in a patient attending routine follow-up with no stated decompensation or metastasis, is localized and potentially curable. A solitary tumour with preserved liver function is treated by resection. Some exam keys favour TACE for a single lesion of 6 cm or more; TACE is not offered, so referral for surgical resection is the answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Systemic therapy is reserved for advanced HCC (vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread); conventional chemotherapy has little role in localized disease.
B. Radiotherapy is not the standard primary treatment of a resectable HCC; it is used selectively when other locoregional options are not possible.
C. Palliative care alone is for end-stage disease (poor performance status or decompensated cirrhosis); this tumour is localized and treatable.
key_concept:
HCC treatment by burden and liver function.
  • Single tumour, preserved liver function: surgical resection
  • Small tumours within transplant criteria with cirrhosis: transplant or ablation
  • Multiple or large unresectable lesions: TACE
  • Vascular invasion or metastasis: systemic therapy
  • End-stage: supportive care
exam_pearl: If TACE is listed for a large or multifocal HCC, it may be the key; if not, choose resection.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): 4×4 hepatocellular carcinoma management? A. chemotherapy / B. Radiotherapy / C. Surgery (highlighted).

stem: An elderly female with DM and HTN is scheduled for elective surgery. BP 160/95 Glucose 9.1 mmol/L What would you do?
OptA: Postpone her surgery for one month
OptB: Adjust her HTN and DM medications
why_right: The lead-in asks what you would do for an elective case in an elderly patient with DM and HTN whose readings are only moderately raised (BP 160/95, glucose 9.1 mmol/L). Neither value signals an active, decompensated problem, so the task is optimization: adjust her antihypertensive and diabetic regimen so she reaches surgery with controlled BP and glucose. Elective surgery is postponed only for decompensated or dangerous states (e.g. volume overload, recent MI, severe hypertension).
why_wrong_block:
A. Postponing for a month is reserved for decompensated conditions (heart failure with volume overload, recent MI, uncontrolled thyroid disease, severe hypertension); these mild elevations do not justify cancelling an elective case.
C. A routine preoperative chest X-ray has no role without cardiorespiratory symptoms or signs; it does not address the abnormal BP and glucose.
D. Baseline bloods (renal function, electrolytes) may well be checked in a diabetic hypertensive, but they are routine work-up, not the action this question targets; the abnormal findings presented are BP and glucose, which need treating.
key_concept:
Elective surgery: optimize controllable comorbidity; delay only for decompensated or high-risk states.
  • Mildly raised BP/glucose: adjust medications, proceed
  • Severe hypertension (≥180/110): defer and control first
  • Volume overload (raised JVP, crackles, edema): delay until optimized
  • Recent MI: delay elective noncardiac surgery (current guidance at least 60 days; older teaching 6 months)
  • Hypo/hyperthyroid: delay until euthyroid
  • Emergency surgery is never delayed for optimization
exam_pearl: Moderate, non-emergent abnormalities = optimize medications; only decompensation earns a postponement.

stem: A 25 year old man presented to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle accident. Initially he was stable then he lost consciousness. Dilated pupils were noted on examination. GCS was 8/15. CT brain shows convex hematoma in the temporal region. What is the appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: convex hematoma in the temporal region
why_right: "Initially stable then lost consciousness" is a lucid interval, and a convex (lens shaped) collection in the temporal region is an epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery. Dilated pupils and GCS 8 mean uncal herniation is under way. An expanding arterial bleed with herniation signs needs emergency craniotomy and evacuation; medical measures only buy minutes.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oxygenation is part of resuscitation (and a GCS of 8 needs a secured airway), but oxygen does not remove the expanding hematoma compressing the brain.
C. Steroids give no benefit in traumatic brain injury and are associated with harm; they help vasogenic edema around tumors, not traumatic bleeds.
D. A shunt treats hydrocephalus (CSF diversion), not an acute extra-axial hematoma causing herniation.
key_concept:
Epidural hematoma with deterioration = emergency craniotomy.
  • Epidural: convex/lens shaped, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • Subdural: concave/crescent, bridging veins, elderly and alcoholics
  • Temporal fracture + lucid interval + ipsilateral blown pupil = epidural
  • Mannitol/hyperventilation: temporizing bridge only
  • GCS ≤8: secure the airway
exam_pearl: Mannitol or hyperventilation may appear as options, but once there is herniation from a surgical lesion the answer is to evacuate it (craniotomy).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Patient presents by ambulance and was intubated; initially was conscious then became unresponsive; CT brain after resuscitation shows convex hematoma. A) Mannitol, B) Hyperventilation, C) Craniotomy [highlighted].

stem: A child had head trauma then went to sleep. When he woke up, he was drowsy and not fully alert. CT showed extracranial hemorrhage after trauma. What is the next step?
highlight_terms_source: head trauma then went to sleep
why_right: The child had head trauma, then "went to sleep" and woke drowsy and not fully alert. That is deterioration after an interval, the classic course of an expanding epidural (extradural) hematoma. With a confirmed post-traumatic bleed and a falling level of consciousness, the source keys immediate craniotomy to evacuate it before herniation occurs.
why_wrong_block:
B. Waiting while the conscious level is falling lets an expanding arterial bleed progress to herniation. Intubation protects the airway but does not treat the lesion.
C. MRI is slow and adds nothing once CT has shown the bleed; it is used for diffuse axonal injury or subtle lesions, not acute surgical hematomas.
D. Observation suits a small hematoma in a child who is fully alert with no neurological deficit; this child is already drowsy.
key_concept:
Post-traumatic intracranial bleed + declining consciousness = surgical evacuation.
  • Lucid interval then drowsiness: epidural hematoma until proven otherwise
  • Small hematoma, alert child, no deficit: observe with serial neuro checks
  • Any deterioration: neurosurgery now
  • CT is the imaging of choice in acute head trauma
exam_pearl: "Went to sleep then woke drowsy" is the lucid-interval story; don't let the vague wording push you to observe.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot inside block 718; 'A. Immediate craniotomy' printed at the bottom of the screenshot as the answer.

stem: A 45 year old woman presented to the Emergency Department after a motor vehicle accident with confusion, headache, and left-sided weakness. GCS is 14/15. CT brain showed a subdural hematoma. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: After an MVA she has a CT-proven subdural hematoma with left-sided weakness (a focal deficit from mass effect) and confusion. GCS 14 does not mean she is safe: a focal deficit shows the hematoma is compressing the brain. The next step is immediate neurosurgical involvement for evacuation, before she deteriorates further.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oxygen supports resuscitation but does nothing for a space-occupying hematoma; she is already maintaining a GCS of 14.
C. High-dose steroids are not used in head injury and are associated with worse outcomes; they suit tumor-related vasogenic edema.
key_concept:
Acute subdural hematoma: whether to operate depends on mass effect and neurological status, not GCS alone.
  • CT: concave/crescent collection, torn bridging veins
  • Thickness >10 mm or midline shift >5 mm: evacuate regardless of GCS
  • GCS falling by 2 or more points, or pupil asymmetry/fixed pupils: evacuate
  • Small, no shift, neurologically intact: observe with serial CT and neuro checks
  • Steroids: no role in traumatic brain injury
exam_pearl: A near-normal GCS with a new focal deficit still makes this a neurosurgical problem; the lateralizing sign outweighs the GCS.

stem: A 65 year old man presented to the Emergency Department with signs of lateralization and GCS 7/15. CT brain shows a 13 mm hematoma with midline shift. The patient was intubated and resuscitated. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: He has signs of lateralization, GCS 7, and a 13 mm hematoma with midline shift, which is significant mass effect. The airway is already secured (intubated and resuscitated), so the next step is definitive: emergency craniotomy and evacuation to relieve the compression.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV mannitol temporarily lowers ICP while theatre is prepared; it does not remove the clot, so it is a bridge, not the management.
C. ICU observation suits a small hematoma without shift in a neurologically stable patient, not a comatose patient with midline shift.
key_concept:
Mass effect + coma + lateralizing signs = evacuate.
  • ABC first: GCS ≤8, intubate
  • Temporizing ICP control: head up, mannitol/hypertonic saline, brief hyperventilation
  • Definitive: craniotomy and hematoma evacuation
  • Observation only for small lesions without shift in a stable patient
exam_pearl: "Intubated and resuscitated" tells you ABC is done; the remaining answer is surgery, not more medical ICP control.

stem: A patient presented after a road-traffic accident with severe injuries. He was unconscious with a GCS of 6. Examination revealed significant instability as well as multiple fractures and other injuries. The patient was hypotensive and tachycardic. What is the Most Appropriate management?
why_right: After an RTA he is hypotensive and tachycardic with an unstable pelvis ("significant instability") and multiple fractures. An unstable pelvic ring bleeding into the pelvis is the likely source of shock. In the circulation step, a pelvic binder is the quick, non-invasive way to reduce pelvic volume and tamponade the bleeding.
why_wrong_block: B. Laparotomy is for unstable blunt trauma with a positive FAST (intraperitoneal blood) or peritonitis. Pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and not controlled by opening the abdomen; laparotomy can make it worse.
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture + shock: binder in the primary survey (C).
  • A: GCS ≤8 needs a definitive airway
  • C: binder over the greater trochanters, transfuse blood products
  • Persistent instability: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing / external fixation
  • Laparotomy only if FAST positive in an unstable patient
exam_pearl: A GCS of 6 means securing the airway comes first in ATLS; between the options listed here, the binder controls the pelvic bleed.

stem: Medium age present with pelvic injury followed by mva Ct showed multiple pelvic injury with severe hematoma and hypotensive patient. What's Next appropriate management after fluid resuscitation?
why_right: CT shows multiple pelvic injuries with a severe hematoma, and the patient is still hypotensive after fluid resuscitation, so he is bleeding from the pelvis. The next step is mechanical: a pelvic binder closes the pelvic ring, reduces its volume and tamponades venous and fracture-site bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
A. An NG tube decompresses the stomach (ileus, obstruction, aspiration risk); it does nothing for hemorrhagic shock.
B. Laparotomy treats intraperitoneal bleeding. A pelvic hematoma is retroperitoneal, and opening the abdomen releases its tamponade.
C. Blood is given alongside the binder in a fluid non-responder, but transfusion only replaces losses; the step keyed here is controlling the source.
key_concept:
Pelvic fracture with ongoing hypotension: stop the bleeding mechanically.
  • Pelvic binder (centered on the greater trochanters)
  • Blood products in parallel
  • Still unstable: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing / external fixation
  • Blood at the urethral meatus: no Foley; do a retrograde urethrogram
exam_pearl: Pelvic hematoma + shock: the answer is a binder, not laparotomy, because laparotomy opens up the retroperitoneal tamponade.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Patient presented to the ER with pelvic fracture, CT scan show he is actively bleeding with a large hematoma in the pelvis, BP = 80/50. Management? A- Emergency laparotomy, B- Transfuse packed red blood cells, C- Pelvic binder [highlighted], D- Reassess.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents to the trauma bay after a motorcycle accident. His blood pressure is 70/30, heart rate is 180 beats/min, and his lactate is 6.0 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior (AP) pelvis reveals an anteroposterior compression (APC) pelvic ring injury. Initial management should include what?
OptB: Obtain a computed tomography (CT) abdomen/pelvis with and without contrast.
why_right: He is in profound hemorrhagic shock (BP 70/30, HR 180, lactate 6.0) with an anteroposterior compression (APC) injury: the open-book pattern that widens the pelvis and tears the posterior venous plexus. A pelvic binder closes the ring early, reduces pelvic volume and helps stabilize him. This is the initial step that targets the source.
why_wrong_block:
A. Massive transfusion will run in parallel in a patient this sick, but it replaces volume without controlling the open-book bleed; the binder is the specific first manoeuvre the question asks for.
B. CT is for hemodynamically stable patients; sending someone with a BP of 70/30 to the scanner is unsafe.
D. Abdominal exploration treats intraperitoneal bleeding (unstable + positive FAST). It does not control pelvic bleeding and releases the retroperitoneal tamponade.
E. CT angiography finds arterial bleeders for embolization, but only once the patient is stable enough to be scanned; it is not the first step in shock.
key_concept:
APC (open-book) pelvic injury in shock: binder first.
  • APC widens pelvic volume and disrupts posterior veins
  • Binder over the greater trochanters
  • Parallel: blood products / massive transfusion protocol
  • Persistent instability: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing
  • CT/CTA only when stable
exam_pearl: "Initial" in an unstable APC pelvis = binder; any option that sends the patient to the scanner is wrong while he is in shock.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot. Correct answer: C. Placement of a pelvic binder early reduces intrapelvic volume and can assist in initial stabilization of the patient.

stem: A man (around 27 years old) presents to the ER after a motorcycle accident. He has multiple pelvic fractures, vascular injuries and he is currently unconscious. What is the most appropriate initial management
why_right: After a motorcycle accident he has multiple pelvic fractures with vascular injuries, which means a major pelvic bleed. The initial step that addresses it is a pelvic binder: it stabilizes the ring, reduces pelvic volume and limits hemorrhage during the circulation stage of the primary survey.
why_wrong_block:
B. Analgesia and IV fluids are supportive. Fluids alone, without source control, dilute clotting factors and do not stop the pelvic bleed.
C. Antibiotics are needed for open fractures, but they are not life-saving in the first minutes of hemorrhage.
key_concept:
Pelvic fracture with bleeding: binder is the first circulation intervention.
  • A: unconscious, so secure the airway
  • C: binder + blood products
  • Unstable despite binder: angioembolization / packing / external fixation
  • Open fracture: antibiotics and tetanus once life threats are controlled
exam_pearl: Unstable hip or pelvis after an RTA is answered with "pelvic binder", not CT, laparotomy or open reduction.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:, continues on next page): RTA patient unstable, low bp, the hip is unstable. What is the initial step? A. Exploratory laparotomy, B. Open reduction, C. pelvic binder [highlighted], D. CT abdomen.

stem: Pt present 5 day after op with foul smelling greenish discharge from surgical wound What's the responsible organism?
why_right: The decisive clue is greenish discharge. Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces blue-green pigments (pyocyanin) and a distinctive odor, so a green, foul-smelling wound discharge points to it. It is a classic pathogen in burns and in moist, hospital-acquired wound infections.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staph aureus is the most common surgical site infection organism overall, but it gives thick creamy-yellow pus, not green discharge.
B. Strep pyogenes causes spreading cellulitis and lymphangitis, often early, with thin serous discharge rather than green pus.
C. Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene: severe pain, crepitus, gas in the tissues and dark "dishwater" discharge after contaminated wounds, not green pus.
key_concept:
Wound discharge color/character points to the organism.
  • Green/blue-green, sweet or foul odor: Pseudomonas
  • Creamy yellow pus: Staph aureus (most common SSI)
  • Rapid spreading cellulitis, red streaks: Strep pyogenes
  • Crepitus, gas, myonecrosis: Clostridium perfringens
  • Prosthetic/graft infection: Staph epidermidis
exam_pearl: "Most common SSI organism" = Staph aureus, but if the stem says green, the answer is Pseudomonas.

stem: Patient with trauma to the thigh about 4cm with visible underline tissues and bone. What is the initial treatment?
OptC: IV antibiotics within the first hour
why_right: This recall's key is a compressive dressing because the very first hands-on step for a large open thigh wound ("4 cm", "visible underlying tissues and bone") is to cover it and control bleeding with direct pressure before anything else is arranged. A sterile, moist pressure dressing stops ongoing blood loss, limits further contamination and is done at the bedside within minutes, while the rest of the open fracture pathway (antibiotics, tetanus, debridement, fixation) follows.
why_wrong_block:
B. Analgesia and fluids are supportive and are given alongside, but they do not address the open wound itself; fluids become the priority only if the patient is in shock.
C. Early IV antibiotics are essential in every open fracture and are started in the ED, but in this recall's logic they follow covering and controlling the wound; they would be the answer if the stem stressed that bleeding is controlled and asked about infection prevention.
D. Debridement and stabilization are the definitive treatment done in theatre after initial ED care (dressing, antibiotics, tetanus, splinting); they are not the initial step.
key_concept:
Open fracture pathway: control bleeding and cover the wound, then IV antibiotics and tetanus, then debridement and irrigation, then fixation.
  • External bleeding: direct pressure first; tourniquet only if pressure fails.
  • Bone visible through a wound = open fracture.
  • IV antibiotics and tetanus are started in the ED, before surgery.
  • Debridement plus irrigation in theatre, then definitive fixation (IM nail for long bones).
  • Splint/realign the limb and recheck distal pulses.
exam_pearl: "Initial" = what you do with your hands at the bedside now; "definitive" = debridement and fixation in theatre.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0379 → C. IV antibiotics within the first hour. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Answer line reads 'A??' (uncertain).

stem: Patient diagnosed with acute pancreatitis 3 weeks ago, now present to ER Complain of mild abdominal pain and tenderness, showed cyst measure 4 cm. How you will manage?
key_concept:
Post-pancreatitis cyst: decide by size, age, symptoms and infection.
  • Under 6 cm, under 6 weeks, minimal symptoms: observe.
  • Over 6 cm, over 6 weeks, growing or symptomatic: endoscopic internal drainage.
  • Infected/abscess (fever, WBC up, gas): percutaneous drainage.
  • Surgery: failed endoscopic drainage or suspected neoplasm.
  • A collection under 4 weeks old is not yet a mature walled pseudocyst.
exam_pearl: Fever or leukocytosis flips any cyst answer to percutaneous drainage; no fever, small and young flips it to observation.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 70y old male patient with prostate cancer undergoing robotic surgery. He is known case of hypertension and had a previous stroke. He is on anticoagulant which was stopped 5 days ago.Which of the following enhances safety of the surgery?
OptC: Check medication cessation and monitor bleeding
highlight_terms_source: on anticoagulant which was stopped 5 days ago
why_right: In a patient on anticoagulation ("stopped 5 days ago") with prior stroke going for major robotic prostatectomy, the safety step is to confirm the drug was actually stopped for the right interval (and coagulation is acceptable) and then watch closely for bleeding. This is part of the pre-op checklist (sign-in/time-out) and directly reduces the main perioperative risk: hemorrhage.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skipping the team briefing removes the checklist step that catches errors such as unchecked anticoagulation; briefing is never skipped.
B. Anesthetic dosing is titrated to the patient, never given "randomly"; underdosing risks awareness and hemodynamic instability.
D. Restarting anticoagulation right before surgery greatly raises bleeding risk; it is resumed after surgery once hemostasis is secure (with bridging decided case by case).
key_concept:
Peri-op anticoagulation safety: confirm cessation, check coagulation, plan when to restart.
  • Verify last dose and that the stopping interval was adequate.
  • Run the surgical safety checklist (sign-in, time-out, sign-out).
  • Anticipate and monitor blood loss intra- and post-op.
  • Restart anticoagulation after surgery when bleeding risk allows; bridging for high thrombotic risk.
exam_pearl: Stroke history tempts you to "protect" with anticoagulation, but pre-op the priority is bleeding control; restart after surgery.

stem: A 2 year old boy his father brought him to the clinic for elective circumcision. What is the best next step?
OptA: Do full investigation including coagulation profile.
OptB: Wait til he became able to make the decision by himself then.
key_concept:
Before circumcision: examine the penis, ask about bleeding, and match setting to age.
  • Hypospadias triad (chordee, hooded foreskin, ventral meatus): never circumcise, refer.
  • Bleeding history positive: coagulation work-up first.
  • Neonate, normal exam: clinic device circumcision under local.
  • Older infant/toddler: theatre under general anesthesia.
exam_pearl: Any penile anomaly on exam makes circumcision contraindicated; the foreskin is saved for repair.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 90 year old male living in residential community comes complaining of severe abdominal pain in the last 24 hours. The abdomen was soft and lax, tender all over, hyperactive abdominal sounds. (no rigidity) What is the next step:
highlight_terms_source: soft and lax, tender all over
key_concept:
Elderly + severe pain + soft, non-rigid abdomen: think mesenteric ischemia or volvulus.
  • Pain out of proportion, AF/vascular risk: CT angiography (not listed).
  • Nursing-home elderly, distension, constipation: abdominal X-ray (coffee bean) then sigmoidoscopic decompression if stable.
  • Peritonitis, gangrene or perforation signs: emergency laparotomy (e.g. Hartmann procedure for gangrenous sigmoid volvulus).
  • Hyperactive bowel sounds can occur early in both ischemia and obstruction.
exam_pearl: Severe pain with a soft, non-rigid abdomen in the elderly is ischemia until proven otherwise; distension plus constipation shifts you to volvulus.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 32 y/o man presents to the ER after a motorcycle accident. He has multiple pelvic fractures, vascular injuries and they did surgery for him What is the most appropriate management post op
why_right: The lead-in is "management post op": the fractures and vascular injuries have already been fixed, so the priority shifts to recovery. Early mobilization and physiotherapy after pelvic fixation reduce DVT, pneumonia, pressure sores and joint stiffness and speed return of function in a young patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. A pelvic binder is a pre-hospital/ED measure to close an unstable pelvic ring and reduce bleeding before definitive fixation; after surgical fixation it has no role.
B. Analgesia and fluids are routine supportive care for every post-op patient, but they are not the specific management goal the question targets; fluids are the answer in the resuscitation phase.
C. Antibiotics are perioperative prophylaxis (or for open fractures/infection); there is no sign of infection here to justify ongoing broad-spectrum cover.
key_concept:
Pelvic trauma by phase: binder and resuscitation pre-op, fixation in theatre, mobilize early post-op.
  • ED: ABC, pelvic binder, blood products, angioembolization or packing if bleeding.
  • Theatre: fixation and vascular repair.
  • Post-op: early mobilization and physiotherapy, VTE prophylaxis, analgesia.
exam_pearl: Read the phase: "post op" removes the binder and resuscitation answers.

stem: Best type of dressing of planter of foot:
key_concept:
Choose the dressing by exudate and infection.
  • Dry/necrotic: hydrogel (adds moisture).
  • Low exudate, clean: hydrocolloid or film.
  • Moderate to heavy exudate: alginate or foam.
  • Infected: frequent-change dressings (gauze) plus treat infection.
  • Diabetic plantar ulcer: offloading matters more than dressing type.
exam_pearl: Wet wound gets an absorber (alginate/foam); dry wound gets a donor (hydrogel).
