stem: DM with ulcer in the foot, what type of dressing?
why_right: Diabetic foot (plantar) ulcers are typically exudative (the embedded version says "plantar ulcer with exudate"), so the dressing should absorb fluid while keeping the bed moist. Alginate turns into a gel as it absorbs exudate, suits moderate to heavy drainage and is easy to change for frequent ulcer inspection.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hydrogel donates moisture to dry or necrotic wounds to soften slough; on an exudative ulcer it adds fluid and macerates the edges.
C. Hydrocolloid is occlusive and suits low exudate, clean wounds; on a diabetic ulcer it may conceal infection and is generally avoided.
D. Transparent film absorbs nothing; it is for dry superficial wounds or IV sites, not an exudative plantar ulcer.
key_concept:
Dressing by exudate: wet wound needs an absorber, dry wound needs moisture.
  • Heavy/moderate exudate: alginate, foam, hydrofiber.
  • Dry/necrotic: hydrogel.
  • Low exudate, clean: hydrocolloid, film.
  • Diabetic foot ulcer care: offloading, debridement, infection control and pulse/vascular check come first.
exam_pearl: If the stem says exudate, pick the absorber (alginate); hydrogel is the trap for dry wounds.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded version: Diabetic patient with plantar ulcer with exudate. Dressing by what? A Hydrocolloid, B Hydrofiber, C Alginate, D Transparent film. Answer: C (Alginate).

stem: A patient with spinal metastasis presents with rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence (level T something). His symptoms continue to worsen despite medical management. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: continue to worsen despite medical management
why_right: This is metastatic spinal cord compression with "rapidly progressive paraparesis" and sphincter loss ("fecal incontinence") that keeps worsening despite medical management (steroids). Progressive deficit despite steroids is the indication for urgent surgical decompression (usually with stabilization, followed by radiotherapy), which gives the best chance of preserving or regaining walking and continence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy acts too slowly to relieve an acute compression; it is used only for very chemosensitive tumors alongside definitive local treatment.
B. Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
C. Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.
key_concept:
Metastatic cord compression: steroids immediately, MRI whole spine, then decompress.
  • Red flags: back pain, leg weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction.
  • Immediate: high-dose dexamethasone.
  • Imaging: urgent MRI whole spine.
  • Progressive deficit, instability or failed medical therapy: urgent surgery then radiotherapy.
  • Unfit for surgery or radiosensitive tumor: radiotherapy.
exam_pearl: Worsening despite steroids is the trigger that turns the answer from radiotherapy/steroids to surgery.

stem: 35 years female presented with appendicitis and she scheduled for laparoscopic Appendectomy, she has history of asthma with no exacerbation. She has fever (>38) Which of the following will improve the surgical safety ?
OptA: Site marking and preparation of surgical equipment
OptB: Pre-op IV antibiotics to accelerate process
OptD: not taking consent it's minor surgery
key_concept:
WHO surgical safety checklist: sign-in, time-out, sign-out.
  • Sign-in: identity, site marking, consent, allergies, airway/aspiration risk, equipment check.
  • Time-out: team introductions, procedure and site confirmed, antibiotics before incision.
  • Sign-out: counts, specimen labelling, post-op concerns.
  • Fever in appendicitis is expected and is not a reason to cancel.
exam_pearl: Options that skip consent, history or briefing are always wrong in safety questions.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. Physical examination reveals a palpable right upper quadrant mass. He has ascites that is well controlled with diuretic therapy. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen demonstrates a 6 × 6 cm mass in the right hepatic lobe with arterial phase enhancement. The portal venous and delayed phases are unremarkable. A biopsy of the lesion confirms hepatocellular carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management step at this stage?
key_concept:
HCC in cirrhosis: treatment follows tumour burden plus liver reserve.
  • Single mass <6 cm, good liver function: surgical resection
  • Single mass ≥6 cm or multiple masses, liver-confined: TACE
  • Within transplant criteria (Milan: single ≤5 cm, or up to 3 lesions ≤3 cm): liver transplant
  • Vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread: systemic therapy
  • Exam habit: if TACE is not among the options for a 6 cm lesion, choose resection
exam_pearl: Two near-identical recalls are keyed differently: the version stressing HBV cirrhosis with controlled ascites is keyed to TACE, while the version stressing a biopsy-proven 6 × 6 cm mass is keyed to resection; read for liver reserve.

stem: A 42-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis evaluated for focal lesion at US abdomen. He is asymptomatic. Currently on diuretics with well-controlled ascites (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values: Hb 110 (130-170 g/L Male; 120-160 g/L Female); Platelets count 123 (150-400 x 109/L); INR 1.5 (0.8-1.2); Total bilirubin 16 (3.5-16.5 mol/L); Aspartate aminotransferase 98 (12-40 IU/L); Alanine aminotransferase 65 (5-40 IU/L); Alkaline phosphatase 120 (39-117 IU/L); Albumin 30 (34-56 g/L). CT scan of liver: Demonstrated a 6 cm lesion with arterial enhancement at RT lobe, portal vein and hepatic veins were patent. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
why_right: A focal arterially enhancing lesion in a hepatitis B cirrhotic liver is HCC. It is a single "6 cm lesion" with "portal vein and hepatic veins patent" (no vascular invasion), so it is intermediate, liver-confined disease. A single mass of 6 cm or more is treated with transarterial chemoembolisation, especially since the liver reserve is reduced (albumin 30, INR 1.5, ascites on diuretics, platelets 123), making resection unsafe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sorafenib is systemic therapy for advanced HCC with vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread; here the veins are patent and the tumour is confined to the liver.
B. Transplant is for HCC within Milan criteria (single lesion ≤5 cm, or up to 3 lesions each ≤3 cm); a single 6 cm lesion is outside them.
C. Resection suits a single mass under 6 cm with well-preserved liver function; this lesion is 6 cm and the patient has ascites, low albumin, raised INR and thrombocytopenia, signs of portal hypertension and limited reserve.
key_concept:
HCC treatment by size and spread:
  • Single mass <6 cm, good liver function: resection
  • Within Milan criteria with cirrhosis: transplant
  • Single mass ≥6 cm or multiple, liver-confined: TACE
  • Vascular invasion or metastasis: sorafenib / systemic therapy
  • Arterial enhancement with washout in a cirrhotic liver is diagnostic without biopsy
exam_pearl: Patent portal and hepatic veins rule out the advanced stage, so a 6 cm single lesion goes to TACE, not sorafenib.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot; answer marked with ** before D.

stem: A patient presents with a mass in the triceps region that has been progressively increasing in size over the past 3 months. MRI findings raise a strong suspicion for malignancy. What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: progressively increasing in size over the past 3 months
why_right: A "progressively increasing" mass in the triceps (a limb soft tissue mass) with MRI "strong suspicion for malignancy" is a suspected soft tissue sarcoma. The biopsy of choice is an image-guided core needle biopsy placed along the line of the future resection: it gives intact tissue for subtype and grade while limiting tumour seeding, and the tract is excised with the definitive operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fine needle aspiration gives only cells without tissue architecture, so it cannot reliably type and grade a sarcoma; it suits cystic or thyroid lesions and lymph nodes.
B. Excising a suspected sarcoma before diagnosis (the unplanned "whoops" excision) leaves inadequate margins and compromises the definitive resection; excisional biopsy suits only small, superficial lesions.
C. Open incisional biopsy contaminates tissue planes and risks haematoma and spillage; it is reserved for when core biopsy is nondiagnostic.
key_concept:
Suspected limb sarcoma pathway:
  • Imaging: MRI of the mass
  • Diagnosis: image-guided core needle biopsy along the planned resection line
  • Staging: CT chest (lungs are the main metastatic site)
  • Incisional biopsy only if core is nondiagnostic
  • Never shell out the mass first
exam_pearl: Large, deep or growing limb mass = sarcoma until proven otherwise; core biopsy, not excision.

stem: A 42-year-old man is involved in a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He presents with shortness of breath, respiratory rate 32/min, and paradoxical chest wall movement. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: "Paradoxical chest wall movement" after high-speed blunt trauma is flail chest (two or more adjacent ribs each fractured in two or more places). The real threat is pain-limited breathing and the underlying pulmonary contusion, so management is supportive: good analgesia and respiratory support (oxygen, escalating to ventilation if he tires or becomes hypoxic, as the RR of 32 suggests may happen).
why_wrong_block:
A. Needle thoracostomy treats tension pneumothorax (hypotension, raised JVP, tracheal shift, hyperresonance); none of those signs are described.
B. A chest tube drains a pneumothorax or haemothorax; flail chest alone does not need one unless an associated air or blood collection is found.
D. A three-sided occlusive dressing is for an open (sucking) chest wound; this is blunt trauma with an intact chest wall.
key_concept:
Chest trauma: match the sign to the fix.
  • Paradoxical movement = flail chest: analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if failing
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Simple pneumothorax or haemothorax: chest tube
  • Open (sucking) wound: three-sided dressing then chest tube
  • Chest tube output >1500 ml initially: thoracotomy
exam_pearl: Flail chest kills through the contusion underneath and hypoventilation from pain, so analgesia is treatment, not comfort.

stem: 65 years old woman came to the ER complaining of sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back Xray: widened mediastinum Dx?
highlight_terms_source: sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back
why_right: "Sudden" severe pain radiating to the back in an older woman plus a "widened mediastinum" on chest X-ray is aortic dissection until proven otherwise. A descending thoracic dissection can present as epigastric or interscapular pain, and mediastinal widening reflects the dilated, dissected aorta. Confirm with CT angiography if stable, or echocardiography if unstable.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oesophageal rupture can widen the mediastinum, but it follows forceful vomiting or endoscopy and shows pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema or pleural effusion; no such history is given.
C. GERD gives burning retrosternal discomfort related to meals and lying down, never sudden severe pain or a widened mediastinum.
D. Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back too, but after gallstones or alcohol, with vomiting and raised lipase; it does not widen the mediastinum.
key_concept:
Back-radiating epigastric/chest pain: the X-ray decides.
  • Widened mediastinum, sudden tearing pain: aortic dissection
  • Pneumomediastinum after vomiting: Boerhaave rupture
  • Normal chest X-ray, gallstones/alcohol, high lipase: pancreatitis
  • Pulsatile abdominal mass: AAA
  • Dissection imaging: CT angiography (stable), echo (unstable)
exam_pearl: Epigastric pain to the back usually says pancreatitis, but a widened mediastinum moves the answer to the aorta.

stem: 72 years old male known to have hypertension and is heavy smoker was found incidentally to have abdominal pulsatile mass. Ultrasound abdomen: 4.5cm abdominal aortic aneurysm Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: An "incidentally" found, asymptomatic 4.5 cm AAA in a man is below the elective repair threshold (5.5 cm in men). The correct plan is surveillance with serial ultrasound to track growth, together with risk factor control (stop smoking, control BP). Repair is triggered by reaching threshold size, rapid growth, symptoms or rupture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simple reassurance ignores a real aneurysm that can grow and rupture; it needs scheduled imaging and risk factor control, not discharge.
B. Urgent surgery is for a symptomatic (tender, painful) or ruptured AAA; elective repair is for ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5 cm in women) or rapid growth. This one is asymptomatic and 4.5 cm.
D. Endarterectomy removes atherosclerotic plaque from a stenosed artery (e.g. carotid); it is not an aneurysm operation. AAA repair is open graft replacement or EVAR.
key_concept:
AAA management by size and symptoms:
  • Asymptomatic, below threshold: ultrasound surveillance + stop smoking + BP control
  • Repair: ≥5.5 cm men, ≥5 cm women, rapid growth, or symptomatic
  • Ruptured / unstable: straight to theatre (bedside US if needed)
  • Initial imaging: ultrasound; stable symptomatic: CT angiography
exam_pearl: Tenderness or pain turns the same 4.5 cm aneurysm into an urgent repair.

stem: A patient with chronic limb ischemia (history of intermittent claudication relieved by rest) presents with acute leg pain and diminished pulses. What is the best initial test?
why_right: Known claudication plus new "acute leg pain and diminished pulses" is acute on chronic limb ischaemia. After starting heparin, the "best initial test" is Doppler ultrasound: it is bedside, fast and non-invasive, confirming loss of arterial flow and locating the occlusion. CT angiography then maps the arteries for revascularisation.
why_wrong_block:
A. ABI is the first test for stable chronic PAD (claudication); in an acute presentation it does not localise the occlusion or guide urgent treatment.
C. MR angiography is slower, less available, and reserved for when iodinated contrast is contraindicated; not an initial test.
D. CT angiography is the confirmatory, gold standard test (the answer to "most appropriate" or "confirmatory" investigation), not the initial one.
key_concept:
Limb ischaemia imaging ladder:
  • Chronic PAD: ABI first, then duplex US, then CT angiography
  • Acute ischaemia: heparin, then Doppler US (initial), then CT angiography (gold standard)
  • Paralysed/threatened limb: skip imaging, go to revascularisation
  • 6 Ps: pain, pallor, paraesthesia, pulselessness, perishing cold, paralysis
exam_pearl: "Initial" = Doppler, "most appropriate/confirmatory" = CT angiography; a paralysed limb gets no imaging at all.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q restatement: K/C DM HTN and PAD, sudden onset leg pain and paresthesia, diminished pulse; most appropriate initial investigation? A. CT Angiography B. ABI C. Doppler. Answer: C (Doppler).

stem: Man presents with progressive shortness of breath for the past 5 days. He was involved in a traffic accident 2 weeks ago. On examination, breath sounds are absent on the right side. with pic of chest X-ray showing a homogenous white appearance on the base of right lung looks like hemothorax. His respiratory rate is 24/min and oxygen saturation is 90% rest of vitals are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: breath sounds are absent on the right side
homogenous white appearance on the base of right lung
why_right: Progressive dyspnoea "2 weeks" after a road traffic accident with "absent breath sounds" on the right and a white (opacified) right base is a delayed traumatic haemothorax, causing hypoxia (SpO2 90%, RR 24). A post-traumatic pleural collection large enough to cause symptoms is drained with a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) after ABCDE, which also lets you measure the blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. There is no fever or infective picture; antibiotics alone would treat empyema or pneumonia but not drain blood compressing the lung.
B. Needle aspiration is used for a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax (and needle decompression for tension pneumothorax with hypotension and tracheal shift); a needle cannot effectively drain a traumatic haemothorax.
D. Thoracic surgery (thoracotomy or VATS) is for massive haemothorax (>1500 ml on tube insertion, or about 200 ml/hour for 2 to 4 hours), instability, or a retained clotted collection after a chest tube, not as the first step.
key_concept:
Traumatic pleural collections:
  • Haemothorax or simple traumatic pneumothorax: ABCDE then chest tube
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Thoracotomy: >1500 ml on insertion, about 200 ml/hour for 2 to 4 hours, or decompensation
  • Retained clotted haemothorax after tube: VATS
exam_pearl: White hemithorax base after trauma = blood; dark hemithorax with no lung markings = air. Both start with a chest tube unless tension.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall mentions a chest X-ray picture, not reproduced on the page.

stem: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents to the emergency department with hypotension and tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: After trauma, "hypotension and tachycardia" is haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock until proven otherwise; it is by far the commonest shock in trauma. Blood loss triggers a reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction (pale, cold peripheries), so start haemorrhage control and blood product resuscitation and look for the bleeding source.
why_wrong_block: A. Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury: loss of sympathetic tone gives hypotension with a normal or slow heart rate and warm, dry peripheries, often with a neurological deficit. Tachycardia argues against it.
key_concept:
Trauma shock by heart rate and skin:
  • Hypotension + tachycardia + cold, pale skin: haemorrhagic shock
  • Hypotension + bradycardia/normal HR + warm skin: neurogenic shock
  • Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds: tamponade
  • Hypotension + raised JVP + tracheal shift: tension pneumothorax
exam_pearl: The heart rate is the switch: fast = bleeding, slow with warm skin = cord injury.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot variant: '72. Pt had RTA he is hypotensive pale and has cold extremities, his HR is 120, what is the diagnosis? A) Neurogenic shock B) Hemorrhagic shock. Answer: B short case like this.'

stem: 67-year-old male presents with hematuria. Known BPH (prostate enlarged on exam, no suspicious features). No trauma, stones, flank pain, or systemic symptoms. IV pyelogram normal. Question: Next diagnostic test?
why_right: Haematuria in a 67-year-old man needs both the upper tract and the bladder examined to exclude malignancy, even with known BPH. The upper tract has already been cleared ("IV pyelogram normal"), and with no stones, flank pain or suspicious prostate, the remaining source to exclude is bladder (urothelial) cancer, which only cystoscopy visualises reliably. BPH is accepted as the cause of haematuria only after this workup.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT (CT urography) images the kidneys and ureters; the upper tract is already covered by the normal pyelogram, and CT misses small flat bladder lesions.
C. Ultrasound assesses kidneys, residual volume and prostate size but is insensitive for small bladder tumours; it does not replace cystoscopy.
D. Prostate biopsy is for a suspicious DRE or raised PSA; the prostate here is benign-feeling with "no suspicious features".
key_concept:
Adult haematuria workup = upper tract imaging + lower tract cystoscopy.
  • Upper tract: CT urography (older exams: IVP) or ultrasound
  • Lower tract: cystoscopy (bladder cancer)
  • Biggest risks: older age, male, smoking
  • Prostate biopsy only for abnormal DRE or raised PSA
  • BPH as the cause is a diagnosis of exclusion
exam_pearl: A normal upper tract study never ends a haematuria workup in an older man; the bladder still needs a scope.

stem: 50 old male age came to the clinic concerned seeing blood in his urine. While obtaining history the patient complained of Right Flank pain. No history of trauma or History Of Prior stones. On examination there's right flank tenderness and enlarged prostate On DRE. Urinalysis : 20 RBC What is The most appropriate investigation
why_right: Hematuria with "right flank pain" and "right flank tenderness" points to an upper tract cause, most commonly a ureteric or renal stone, even with no prior stones. Non-contrast CT KUB is the first line and most accurate imaging for suspected urolithiasis: it detects almost all stones regardless of composition and shows size, site, hydronephrosis and alternative causes. The enlarged prostate is a distractor; it does not explain flank pain.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cystoscopy looks at the bladder and urethra; it is the test for painless hematuria in an older patient (bladder cancer workup), not the first test when flank pain points to the kidney or ureter.
C. Plain X-ray KUB misses radiolucent (uric acid), small or overlying stones; it is used to follow known radiopaque stones, not to make the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Flank pain + hematuria = stone until proven otherwise: image with non-contrast CT KUB.
  • Suspected stone: non-contrast CT KUB (contrast can hide stones)
  • Pregnancy or children: ultrasound first
  • X-ray KUB: follow-up of known radiopaque stones
  • Painless hematuria in older adult: cystoscopy plus upper tract imaging
  • BPH symptoms alone: alpha blocker, cystoscopy only if bladder pathology suspected
exam_pearl: Painful (flank) hematuria = CT KUB; painless hematuria in an older man = think bladder cancer and cystoscopy.

stem: An patient had a sigmoid polyp and was removed completely by endoscopy, which of the following will indicates the highest malignant transformation?
why_right: The question asks which histology carries the "highest malignant transformation". Among colorectal polyps, villous adenoma has the greatest malignant potential, ranking above tubulovillous and tubular adenomas, while hyperplastic polyps are non-neoplastic.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tubular adenoma is the most common adenoma but has the lowest malignant risk of the three adenoma types (ranks third).
C. Hyperplastic polyps are non-neoplastic and carry the lowest risk of all the options.
D. Tubulovillous adenoma has intermediate risk (ranks second), below a pure villous adenoma.
key_concept:
Malignant potential rises with the villous component.
  • 1) Villous adenoma: highest
  • 2) Tubulovillous adenoma
  • 3) Tubular adenoma
  • 4) Hyperplastic polyp: non-neoplastic, lowest
  • Size and high-grade dysplasia also raise risk
exam_pearl: Tubular = most common adenoma; villous = most malignant. Do not swap them.

stem: An adult, medically free patient presents with upper abdominal pain for 12 hours associated with nausea, but no vomiting. There are no changes in stool or urine color, no pale stools or dark urine, and no changes in bowel habits. On examination, sclera and skin are normal. On deep palpation there is tenderness. Vital signs: normal Ultrasound findings: • Multiple gallbladder stones • Normal gallbladder wall thickness • No pericholecystic fluid • Common bile duct (CBD) is obstructed by a stone Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Common bile duct (CBD) is obstructed by a stone
why_right: A gallstone obstructing the "common bile duct" with 12 hours of upper abdominal pain, nausea and deep tenderness is the classic setup for gallstone (biliary) pancreatitis, the most common cause of acute pancreatitis. The other options are excluded by the stem: normal gallbladder wall and no pericholecystic fluid argue against cholecystitis, and normal sclera and skin with no dark urine or pale stool argue against obstructive jaundice. The diagnosis is confirmed with lipase or amylase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Acute cholecystitis needs ultrasound signs of inflammation (thick gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid) plus fever and RUQ tenderness; here the wall is normal, there is no fluid and vitals are normal.
C. Obstructive jaundice would show yellow sclera, dark urine, pale stools and itching; the stem explicitly says sclera and skin are normal with no urine or stool change.
D. Small bowel obstruction presents with colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation; this patient has no vomiting and no change in bowel habit, and ultrasound shows a biliary cause.
key_concept:
Gallstones on US: read the findings to name the complication.
  • Stones only, short pain, no signs: biliary colic
  • Thick wall + pericholecystic fluid + fever: acute cholecystitis
  • CBD stone + jaundice, dark urine, pale stool: choledocholithiasis / obstructive jaundice
  • Jaundice + fever + RUQ pain: ascending cholangitis
  • CBD stone + epigastric pain, no jaundice: gallstone pancreatitis (confirm with lipase)
exam_pearl: Pancreatitis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, lipase/amylase ≥3 times normal, imaging; a CBD stone with epigastric pain points there.

stem: 50 years old have pancreatitis 6 weeks ago came with worsening abdominal pain and palpable enlarging mass. CT scan : well defined fluid cyst. Most appropriate management ?
why_right: A "well defined fluid cyst" appearing "6 weeks" after pancreatitis is a pancreatic pseudocyst. It is symptomatic ("worsening abdominal pain") and growing ("palpable enlarging mass"), and it is at least 6 weeks old, so it meets the criteria for drainage. With no fever or leukocytosis to suggest infection, endoscopic internal drainage into the stomach or duodenum is the treatment of choice.
why_wrong_block:
B. IV antibiotics treat infection; there is no fever, leukocytosis or gas in the collection, and antibiotics do not decompress a pseudocyst.
C. Antibiotics plus observation is wrong twice: no infection is present, and observation is only for small, asymptomatic or early collections, not an enlarging symptomatic one.
D. Surgical drainage (cystgastrostomy) is reserved for failure or unsuitability of endoscopic drainage; it is not first line and not "immediate".
key_concept:
Post-pancreatitis collection: decide by size, age, symptoms and infection.
  • Pseudocyst: homogeneous, thin-walled, more than 4 weeks after pancreatitis; CT is the best imaging
  • Small, asymptomatic or under 6 weeks: observe
  • Over 6 cm, over 6 weeks, symptomatic or growing: endoscopic drainage
  • Infected pseudocyst or abscess (fever, high WBC, gas): percutaneous drainage first
  • Surgery: after failed minimally invasive drainage
exam_pearl: Same cyst plus fever and high WBC = abscess or infected collection, and the answer flips to percutaneous drainage.

stem: A young girl with RLQ abdominal pain, afebrile, normal WBC, mild tenderness, question specifically says: what is the most important management to avoid missed diagnosis?
OptA: Admit for serial abdominal examination and reassessment for 24 hours
OptB: Discharge and ask her to come back if pain returned
why_right: An "afebrile" girl with RLQ pain, "normal WBC" and only "mild tenderness" is an equivocal case of possible early appendicitis. The lead-in asks how to "avoid missed diagnosis": the safest strategy is admission for active observation with repeated abdominal examination by the same team, which reveals evolving appendicitis while avoiding an unnecessary operation. In a girl, a pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound are usually added during this period.
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharging an equivocal RLQ pain risks missing early appendicitis that progresses to perforation; discharge with return advice fits only clearly non-surgical, resolving pain.
C. Analgesia should be given and does not mask appendicitis, but on its own it does not establish or exclude the diagnosis; it is part of care, not the strategy that prevents a miss.
key_concept:
Equivocal RLQ pain: observe, re-examine, then decide.
  • Clear clinical appendicitis: surgery
  • Equivocal (mild signs, normal WBC, afebrile): admit, serial exams and labs
  • Female: pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound (torsion, ovarian cyst, ectopic)
  • Children and pregnancy: ultrasound first; CT if still unclear in adults
  • Analgesia is safe and does not hide peritonitis
exam_pearl: Serial examination is the best tool for an unclear appendix; analgesia is safe and should never be withheld while observing.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with recent history of feeling tiredness, fatigue and weight loss. She noticed as well worsening of her chronic constipation. Stool for occult blood was positive (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values RBC 3 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 89 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) HCT 0.25 0.42-0.52 (Male) 0.37-0.48 (Female) Platelets count 234 150-400 × 109/L Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Stool for occult blood was positive
why_right: A "60-year-old" with fatigue, weight loss, worsening constipation (change in bowel habit), anemia (Hb 89) and a positive stool occult blood test has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. Colonoscopy is the best next step because it visualizes the entire colon and allows biopsy and removal of polyps in the same session.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT enterography images the small bowel (Crohn disease, obscure small bowel bleeding) and cannot take tissue; it is not the test for a suspected colon cancer.
B. Barium enema is outdated, misses small lesions and cannot biopsy; it is used only when colonoscopy is impossible.
C. Sigmoidoscopy sees only the distal colon and would miss a right-sided cancer, which typically causes anemia; a positive occult blood test needs full colonoscopy.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT/FIT or iron deficiency anemia with red flags = colonoscopy.
  • Colonoscopy: whole colon + biopsy + polypectomy
  • Sigmoid cancer found on sigmoidoscopy: still need full colonoscopy for synchronous lesions
  • After diagnosis: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
  • Barium enema or CT colonography: only if colonoscopy not possible
exam_pearl: Never repeat a positive occult blood test or settle for a partial exam; go to colonoscopy.

stem: Patient presented with weight loss (and other dyspepsia Symptoms) Gastric antrum Histopathology confirmed Adenocarcinoma. How to stage the “T”?
why_right: The lead-in asks specifically how to stage the "T", which is the depth of tumour invasion through the gastric wall layers. Endoscopic ultrasound resolves the individual wall layers and nearby nodes, so it is the most accurate test for T (and local N) staging of gastric cancer. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is still done first overall to look for distant metastases (M).
why_wrong_block:
B. Transabdominal ultrasound cannot resolve the layers of the stomach wall; at most it may show liver metastases or ascites.
C. A nuclear (bone) scan looks for skeletal metastases when symptoms suggest them; it says nothing about depth of invasion.
D. A contrast (Gastrografin) study outlines the lumen and mucosa or shows a leak, but cannot measure how deep the tumour penetrates the wall.
key_concept:
TNM staging tools for upper GI cancer.
  • Diagnosis: upper endoscopy with biopsy
  • M (distant spread): CT chest, abdomen and pelvis first
  • T and local N: endoscopic ultrasound
  • Occult peritoneal disease: staging laparoscopy
  • PET-CT: occult distant metastases (more in esophageal cancer)
exam_pearl: "Next investigation after biopsy" = CT CAP; "how to assess T / depth of invasion" = EUS.

stem: A 62-year-old man has been noticing progressive difficulty swallowing, first solid food and now liquids as well. A barium study shows a ragged narrowing just below the carinal level. Endoscopic biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following provides the most accurate information regarding the T stage of an esophageal carcinoma?
highlight_terms_source: T stage of an esophageal carcinoma
why_right: The lead-in asks for "the most accurate information regarding the T stage", which is depth of invasion through the esophageal wall. Endoscopic ultrasound visualizes each wall layer and periesophageal nodes, making it the most accurate test for T (and local N) staging of esophageal cancer once biopsy has confirmed the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is the first staging scan for distant metastases and gross invasion of neighbouring organs, but it cannot separate the wall layers to define early T stage.
B. PET is best for detecting occult distant metastases (M stage); its spatial resolution is too low to judge depth of wall invasion.
C. MRI is not a routine staging tool for esophageal cancer and is less accurate than EUS for wall depth.
E. Bronchoscopy checks for tracheobronchial invasion in tumours at or above the carina; it shows airway involvement, not the tumour's depth in the esophageal wall.
key_concept:
Esophageal cancer workup: biopsy, then stage in layers.
  • Diagnosis: endoscopy with biopsy (barium shows a ragged stricture)
  • Distant spread: CT chest and abdomen, then PET-CT
  • T and local N: endoscopic ultrasound
  • Upper or mid tumour near the airway: bronchoscopy for tracheal invasion
  • SCC: upper/mid esophagus, smoking, alcohol, achalasia; adenocarcinoma: lower, Barrett, GERD
exam_pearl: T = EUS, M = CT/PET; bronchoscopy only answers "is the airway invaded".

stem: Case Of Post-Operative Fever - 4 days post abdominal surgery, pale, hypotensive with cold extremities. how to confirm iV fluid level in patient who is being treated for dehydration?
why_right: This recall's key is CVP 8 because the question asks how to confirm the "IV fluid level" (intravascular filling) in a hypovolemic patient, and CVP is the classic direct estimate of right-sided filling pressure. A CVP of 8 sits in the traditional resuscitation target range of 8 to 12 mmHg, whereas each of the other values is either clearly abnormal or a perfusion marker rather than a volume measure.
why_wrong_block:
B. A MAP of 45 is profound hypotension; the usual resuscitation target is a MAP of at least 65, so this value shows ongoing shock, not adequate fluid.
C. Urine output of 0.1 mL/kg/h is severe oliguria; adequate resuscitation is shown by at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults.
D. Lactate reflects tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism rather than intravascular volume, and a value of 2 sits at the upper limit of normal, so on this key's logic it does not confirm fluid status.
key_concept:
Resuscitation endpoints: know the target for each number.
  • CVP: traditional target 8 to 12 mmHg (static, limited predictor)
  • MAP: at least 65 mmHg
  • Urine output: at least 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, at least 1 mL/kg/h children
  • Lactate: normal up to 2 mmol/L; falling lactate = improving perfusion
  • Burns: urine output is the main endpoint
exam_pearl: The same four options appear in a burn recall keyed to lactate 2; read whether the question asks for "fluid level" (CVP here) or "good resuscitation".

stem: Patient came to ER with burns all over the body after intubation and resuscitation what will indicate good fluid…
why_right: After intubation and resuscitation of extensive burns, the question asks which value indicates "good fluid" resuscitation. Urine output is the usual burn endpoint, but here it is only 0.1 mL/kg/h, so the remaining sign of adequate tissue perfusion is a lactate of 2, which is at the upper limit of normal and shows no significant anaerobic metabolism. CVP is unreliable in burns and MAP 45 is shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine output is the best burn endpoint, but the target is at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (1 mL/kg/h in children); 0.1 mL/kg/h means under-resuscitation.
B. A MAP of 45 is severe hypotension and indicates inadequate resuscitation; the target is a MAP of at least 65.
C. CVP is invasive and a poor predictor of volume status in burns, where massive capillary leak and fluid shifts distort it; it is not used as the resuscitation endpoint.
key_concept:
Burn resuscitation: titrate fluids to perfusion endpoints.
  • Main endpoint: urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, 1 mL/kg/h children
  • Supporting: normal or falling lactate
  • Heart rate and BP: unreliable (pain, catecholamines)
  • CVP: poor predictor, not a target
  • Fluid: Ringer lactate by Parkland formula, then adjust to urine output
exam_pearl: If the urine output option is below target, pick the next perfusion marker that is normal (lactate), not CVP.

stem: 10 years old girl came to the ER complaining from RLQ abdominal pain that associated with nausea and 3 times vomiting, there is pain and rebound tenderness in examination. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A school-age child with RLQ pain, nausea and vomiting, and rebound tenderness on examination has the classic picture of acute appendicitis. Rebound tenderness signals localized peritoneal irritation in the right iliac fossa, which fits an inflamed appendix. In a child, ultrasound is the first imaging if confirmation is needed, followed by appendectomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intussusception: typically an infant or toddler (about 6 months to 3 years) with episodic colicky crying, drawing up the legs, a sausage-shaped mass and red currant jelly stool; a 10-year-old with localized RLQ peritonism does not fit.
C. Meckel's diverticulum: classically presents in young children with painless rectal bleeding; Meckel's diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis but is far rarer, so it is not the diagnosis for this classic picture.
key_concept:
RLQ pain + nausea/vomiting + rebound tenderness = acute appendicitis until proven otherwise.
  • Pain often starts periumbilical, then migrates to the RLQ
  • Anorexia, low-grade fever, McBurney point tenderness, Rovsing sign
  • Imaging: US in children and pregnancy; CT best in non-pregnant adults
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
exam_pearl: Age flips the answer: infant with colicky pain and a mass = intussusception; toddler with painless bleeding = Meckel's; school-age child with RLQ peritonism = appendicitis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A 'Q:' variant: 14 years old female with periumbilical pain shifting to the right, anorexia, mild diarrhea + dysuria, no vomiting/fever, right tenderness increasing with cough; options Appendicitis / Gastroenteritis / Right ureteric stone / UTI; highlighted A) Appendicitis.

stem: 90 year old male living in residential community comes complaining of severe abdominal pain in the last 24 hours. The abdomen was soft and lax, tender all over, hyperactive abdominal sounds. (no rigidity) What is the next step:
highlight_terms_source: soft and lax, tender all over
why_right: A 90-year-old from a residential (care) home with diffuse tenderness, a soft, lax abdomen with no rigidity and hyperactive bowel sounds needs a complete bedside examination before any test, and that includes a digital rectal examination. In frail, immobile elderly patients DRE quickly detects fecal impaction (a common cause of pain and obstructive symptoms), rectal masses and blood (hinting at ischemia or malignancy). It is cheap, immediate and guides the choice of further investigation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy: an elective, preparation-requiring investigation, not the next step in acute severe abdominal pain; it is used for bleeding or suspected colorectal cancer once the acute picture is clarified.
B. Sigmoidoscopy: useful for suspected sigmoid volvulus (huge tympanic distension, coffee bean sign) or distal lesions, but should follow examination, not replace it.
C. US abdomen: reasonable imaging for biliary or pelvic causes, but the bedside examination (including DRE) is completed first; in a frail elderly patient with diffuse pain, CT is usually the more informative imaging.
key_concept:
Acute abdomen in the elderly: complete the examination (including DRE) before imaging.
  • Nursing home + immobility: think fecal impaction
  • DRE: impaction, rectal mass, blood on the glove
  • Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen: think mesenteric ischemia (CT angiography)
  • Massive tympanic distension + coffee bean sign: sigmoid volvulus (sigmoidoscopic decompression)
exam_pearl: Soft, non-rigid abdomen in an elderly patient does not exclude serious pathology; the elderly often lack peritoneal signs.

stem: 32 years old male admitted for motor vehicle accident, after initially stabilization and multiple surgical interventions for fractures. He is in pos-op care Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measures?
why_right: After major trauma and multiple fracture surgeries, the main preventable complications are those of immobility: DVT/PE, pneumonia and atelectasis, pressure ulcers, muscle wasting and joint stiffness. Early mobilization and physiotherapy address all of these, which is why it is the most appropriate preventive measure in the post-operative phase (alongside pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis when bleeding risk allows).
why_wrong_block:
A. Extended bed rest: increases the risk of DVT/PE, pneumonia, pressure sores and deconditioning; it is the opposite of prevention.
B. High-dose corticosteroids: no preventive role after trauma surgery; they impair wound and fracture healing and raise infection risk.
D. Empirical antibiotics for 5 days: surgical prophylaxis is short (a single pre-incision dose, at most about 24 h for closed fractures); prolonged empirical courses promote resistance and C. difficile without benefit.
key_concept:
Post-operative prevention after polytrauma = fight immobility.
  • Early mobilization and physiotherapy
  • VTE prophylaxis: LMWH when bleeding risk allows, mechanical devices otherwise
  • Incentive spirometry / chest physiotherapy against atelectasis and pneumonia
  • Pressure area care
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: short, peri-incisional only
exam_pearl: Bed rest is never the preventive answer post-op; mobilization is.

stem: A 25-year-old patient sustained a blunt trauma to the right chest wall; there was paradoxical movement of the right side of the chest (see report). Heart rate 96 /min Respiratory rate 35 /min Oxygen saturation 84 % Chest X-ray: Fracture 2nd through 4th ribs at more than 1 site. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: Fracture 2nd through 4th ribs at more than 1 site
why_right: Ribs 2 to 4 fractured at more than one site with paradoxical chest movement is flail chest. The danger is hypoxia from the unstable segment and the underlying pulmonary contusion, here shown by SpO2 84% and RR 35. Initial management is supportive: adequate analgesia plus oxygenation and assisted ventilation, with intubation when hypoxia persists (SpO2 below about 88% is a trauma intubation trigger).
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid resuscitation: the patient is not hypotensive (HR 96, no shock); the problem is respiratory, and excess fluid worsens pulmonary contusion. Fluids would lead if he were in hemorrhagic shock.
C. Needle decompression: treats tension pneumothorax (hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension), none of which is described.
D. Thoracostomy chest tube: for pneumothorax or hemothorax seen on examination or X-ray; the film here shows only rib fractures.
key_concept:
Flail chest = 2 or more adjacent ribs fractured in 2 or more places + paradoxical movement.
  • Problem: hypoxia from the flail segment and pulmonary contusion
  • Treatment: analgesia (including regional blocks), oxygen, assisted ventilation
  • Intubate if hypoxia persists or respiratory failure develops
  • Avoid fluid overload (contusion worsens)
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
exam_pearl: Paradoxical movement means flail chest (ventilate and give analgesia); hyperresonance with tracheal shift means tension pneumothorax (decompress).
compiler_note: Compiler note: A second version (option B 'Assistant ventilation') also gives 'Answer: B'.

stem: Pelvic fracture with BP 88/55. Next step?
why_right: A pelvic fracture with BP 88/55 means hemorrhagic shock from pelvic bleeding, which can be massive. Current trauma resuscitation favors early blood products (balanced transfusion) over large-volume crystalloid in a hypotensive bleeding trauma patient, together with a pelvic binder and definitive hemorrhage control (angioembolization or preperitoneal packing). The key here is therefore blood transfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bed rest: appropriate only for a stable, minor (e.g. pubic ramus) fracture; useless in a hypotensive patient.
B. Laparotomy: pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and is not controlled by laparotomy; laparotomy is for intra-abdominal bleeding with a positive FAST in an unstable patient.
C. IV fluids: a limited initial crystalloid bolus may be given while blood is prepared, but large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding; ongoing shock from pelvic hemorrhage needs blood.
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture = hemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise.
  • Pelvic binder to close the pelvic volume
  • Early blood products (massive transfusion protocol if needed)
  • Limit crystalloid
  • Hemorrhage control: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing / external fixation
  • Positive FAST + unstable: laparotomy for the abdomen, not the pelvis
exam_pearl: If 'pelvic binder' appears among the options, it usually comes first; otherwise blood beats crystalloid in hemorrhagic shock.

stem: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s file before surgery and notices that the allergy history is not documented. According to the surgical safety checklist, at which stage should allergies be confirmed?
why_right: In the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, Sign In is done before induction of anesthesia and includes confirming identity, site, procedure and consent, the site marking, the anesthesia safety check, pulse oximetry, and explicitly "Does the patient have a known allergy?", along with airway and blood-loss risk. Allergies must be known before any anesthetic agent or antibiotic is given, so they are confirmed at Sign In.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sign Out: done before the patient leaves the operating room; it covers the procedure name, instrument, sponge and needle counts, specimen labeling, equipment problems and recovery concerns.
C. Time Out: done before skin incision; the team introduces itself, reconfirms patient, site and procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 60 minutes, anticipated critical events and imaging. Allergy is checked earlier, before induction.
D. Postoperative: not a phase of the checklist, and too late; anesthetic drugs and antibiotics would already have been given.
key_concept:
WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: 3 phases.
  • Sign In (before induction): identity, site, consent, site marking, anesthesia check, oximeter, allergy, airway/aspiration risk, blood-loss risk
  • Time Out (before incision): team introductions, confirm patient/site/procedure, antibiotics within 60 min, critical events, imaging
  • Sign Out (before leaving OR): procedure recorded, counts, specimen labeling, equipment issues, recovery plan
exam_pearl: Allergy, airway and blood-loss risk = Sign In; antibiotics within 60 minutes = Time Out; counts and specimens = Sign Out.

stem: A 28 year old female presented following radiation of neck with neck swelling. Ultrasound showed swelling in the left lobe of the thyroid of 3x4cm of papillary thyroid cancer. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: This is confirmed papillary thyroid cancer (3x4 cm) in a patient with a history of neck radiation. Prior head and neck irradiation raises the risk of multifocal and bilateral disease, and is a standard indication for total thyroidectomy rather than lobectomy, even for a tumor that would otherwise allow a lobectomy. Total thyroidectomy also allows radioactive iodine therapy and thyroglobulin surveillance afterwards.
why_wrong_block:
A. Left lobectomy: an option for low-risk, unifocal differentiated cancer (roughly 1 to 4 cm) without risk factors, or for an indeterminate Bethesda IV nodule; the radiation history removes this option.
B. Left lobectomy with isthmusectomy: still a unilateral procedure, with the same limitation as lobectomy; it leaves the contralateral lobe at risk in a radiation-exposed gland.
C. Subtotal thyroidectomy: leaves residual thyroid tissue, which is inadequate oncologically and interferes with radioactive iodine; it is an old operation for benign goiter or Graves disease.
key_concept:
Differentiated thyroid cancer: extent of surgery.
  • <1 cm, low risk: active surveillance or lobectomy
  • 1 to 4 cm, low risk: lobectomy or total thyroidectomy
  • >4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, nodal or distant metastases, prior radiation, bilateral nodules: total thyroidectomy
  • Bethesda VI (malignant): near-total / total thyroidectomy
  • Medullary cancer: total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: History of neck irradiation pushes any thyroid cancer toward total thyroidectomy.

stem: An elderly man with a known history of BPH presents to OPD with difficult urination, frequency, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has been treated with an alpha-blocker for the past 2 years, with persistent symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Adjust the dose of the alpha-blocker
highlight_terms_source: alpha-blocker for the past 2 years, with persistent symptoms
why_right: BPH is treated initially with an alpha-blocker, and TURP is the definitive treatment when medical therapy fails. Here the man has been on an alpha-blocker for 2 years with persistent symptoms (hesitancy, frequency, urgency, incomplete emptying), which is failure of medical therapy, so the most appropriate next step among these options is TURP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adjust the alpha-blocker dose: alpha-blockers have a quick, largely dose-limited effect; after 2 years of persistent symptoms, a higher dose adds side effects (orthostatic hypotension) without meaningful benefit.
B. Suprapubic catheterization: used for acute retention when urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated (e.g. urethral trauma or stricture); this patient is voiding, not in retention.
C. Clean intermittent catheterization: for neurogenic bladder or chronic retention in patients unfit for surgery; it is not the next step for symptomatic BPH failing medication.
key_concept:
BPH management ladder.
  • Initial: lifestyle measures + alpha-blocker (tamsulosin, doxazosin)
  • Large gland: add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride)
  • Failed medical therapy or complications (retention, recurrent UTI, stones, hematuria, renal impairment): TURP
  • Very large gland: open or enucleation prostatectomy
  • Acute retention: Foley catheter + urine culture
exam_pearl: New LUTS with an enlarged prostate = alpha-blocker; persistent symptoms despite long medical treatment = TURP.

stem: A patient with spinal metastasis presents with rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence (level T something). His symptoms continue to worsen despite medical management. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence
continue to worsen despite medical management
why_right: This is metastatic spinal cord compression with "rapidly progressive paraparesis" and sphincter loss ("fecal incontinence") that keeps worsening despite medical management (steroids). Progressive deficit despite steroids is the indication for urgent surgical decompression (usually with stabilization, followed by radiotherapy), which gives the best chance of preserving or regaining walking and continence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy acts too slowly to relieve an acute compression; it is used only for very chemosensitive tumors alongside definitive local treatment.
B. Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
C. Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.
key_concept:
Metastatic cord compression: steroids immediately, MRI whole spine, then decompress.
  • Red flags: back pain, leg weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction.
  • Immediate: high-dose dexamethasone.
  • Imaging: urgent MRI whole spine.
  • Progressive deficit, instability or failed medical therapy: urgent surgery then radiotherapy.
  • Unfit for surgery or radiosensitive tumor: radiotherapy.
exam_pearl: Worsening despite steroids is the trigger that turns the answer from radiotherapy/steroids to surgery.

stem: Pts in the 4th post op day complaining of fever only what is the best next ?
why_right: By the postoperative fever timeline, fever on days 4 to 5 points to surgical site (wound) infection or DVT. On the 4th post-op day with fever as the only complaint, the best next step is to examine the wound for redness, warmth, discharge or collection; if infection is found, the wound is opened and drained.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: may support infection but does not localize the source; the decisive next step is the targeted bedside examination of the surgical site.
B. Urine culture: UTI is the classic cause on days 2 to 3 (especially after catheterization); on day 4 the wound comes first.
D. Review medication: drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion, considered later when no infectious source is found.
key_concept:
Post-operative fever by day.
  • Day 1: atelectasis (or early necrotizing wound infection)
  • Days 2 to 3: UTI, superficial thrombophlebitis, pneumonia
  • Days 4 to 5: surgical site infection, DVT
  • Day 6 and beyond: wound dehiscence, deep collection or abscess (CT)
  • SSI management: open the wound and drain; CT if deep infection suspected
exam_pearl: Day 3 fever pushes you to the urine; day 4 to 5 fever pushes you to the wound.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler note: It Was "Wound Exploration", Not "Wound Assessment".

stem: A 70-year-old female presents with a complaint of rectal pain and passing mucus. This exact picture was shown: What is the diagnosis?
why_right: The image shows circumferential, concentric mucosal folds protruding through the anus in a 70-year-old woman with mucus discharge and rectal discomfort. Full-thickness rectal prolapse is typical of elderly women (weak pelvic floor, chronic straining), and the exposed mucosa secretes mucus. Concentric rings indicate the whole rectal wall has prolapsed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin tag: a small, soft, skin-covered flap at the anal verge, often painless or linked to a fissure; it is not a mucosal, circumferential protrusion.
C. Haemorrhoid: prolapsed hemorrhoids appear as separate cushions with radial grooves between them, and classically present with painless bright red bleeding, not concentric circular folds.
key_concept:
Anal protrusion: read the folds.
  • Concentric (circular) folds: full-thickness rectal prolapse
  • Radial folds, separate cushions: prolapsed hemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse
  • Small skin-covered tag: skin tag (sentinel tag with a posterior fissure)
  • Rectal prolapse: elderly women, straining, mucus, incontinence
  • Treatment: surgical (perineal approach in frail elderly, abdominal rectopexy if fit)
exam_pearl: Concentric rings = rectal prolapse; radial grooves = hemorrhoids.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Photo shows circumferential concentric mucosal folds protruding from the anus.

stem: Patient in 60s diagnosed with prostate cancer presenting with back pain (and maybe lower limb weakness). What is the appropriate next step for him?
why_wrong_block:
A. IV hydrocortisone captures the steroid idea, but the steroid of choice for cord edema is dexamethasone, and steroid alone without urgent MRI leaves the level and cause of compression undefined.
B. MRI is the right test, but outpatient timing is wrong: suspected cord compression needs same-day imaging, because delay risks permanent paralysis and sphincter loss. Outpatient MRI suits chronic mechanical back pain without red flags.
key_concept:
Back pain in a patient with cancer = spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.
  • Commonest culprits: prostate, breast, lung (bone metastases to spine)
  • Immediate: high-dose IV dexamethasone
  • Imaging: urgent whole spine MRI (not outpatient)
  • Definitive: radiotherapy or surgical decompression after MRI
  • A normal neuro exam does not exclude impending compression
exam_pearl: Right idea, wrong detail: hydrocortisone instead of dexamethasone, or MRI booked outpatient, are both traps in a cancer patient with back pain.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Both options crossed out with pen X marks. Embedded AI note: suspected spinal cord compression (oncologic emergency); neither A nor B correct; correct: urgent (not outpatient) whole spine MRI and high-dose IV corticosteroids, typically dexamethasone not hydrocortisone. Outpatient MRI inappropriate given urgency.
Other marked answers: Screenshot Answer line: A (IV hydrocortisone)

stem: A young man was brought to the Emergency Department after he was hit in the chest while playing football. On examination, he was dyspneic and drowsy with GCS 11/15. Tracheal shifting to the left and raised JVP were noted. He has barely audible breath sounds on the right side. Blood pressure 80/50 mmHg Heart rate 130 /min Respiratory rate 32 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 90% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: barely audible breath sounds on the right side
why_right: After a chest blow, this man has barely audible breath sounds on the right, trachea shifted to the left (away from the silent side), raised JVP and shock (BP 80/50, HR 130). That combination of unilateral silent chest, contralateral tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and hypotension is a right tension pneumothorax, an obstructive shock needing immediate decompression.
why_wrong_block:
A. Flail segment needs multiple rib fractures with paradoxical chest wall movement; it causes hypoxia and pain but does not shift the trachea or raise the JVP.
B. Cardiac tamponade also gives raised JVP and hypotension (Beck triad with muffled heart sounds), but breath sounds stay equal and the trachea stays central; it is typical of penetrating injury.
C. Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia and crackles developing over hours, but no tracheal deviation, raised JVP or obstructive shock.
key_concept:
Raised JVP + hypotension after chest trauma: decide tension vs tamponade by the lungs and trachea.
  • Tension pneumothorax: silent hyperresonant side, trachea shifted away, raised JVP, shock
  • Tamponade: equal breath sounds, central trachea, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus
  • Massive hemothorax: silent DULL side, flat neck veins
  • Flail chest: paradoxical segment, supportive care
  • Tension treatment: needle decompression then chest tube (clinical diagnosis, no X-ray first)
exam_pearl: Silent side + distended neck veins = tension; silent side + flat neck veins and dullness = massive hemothorax.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: MVA with distended neck vein, trachea shifted to the other side, absent sound, hyperresonance on percussion, BP 80/60; options Cardiac tamponade / Massive hemithorax / Tension pneumothorax (highlighted, consistent).

stem: Lesser sac 9 cm cyst posterior to the stomach
highlight_terms_source: 9 cm cyst posterior to the stomach
key_concept:
Lesser sac cyst behind the stomach: the history and cyst features decide pseudocyst versus neoplasm.
  • Pseudocyst: homogenous, thin wall, more than 4 weeks after pancreatitis; CT is the best imaging
  • Small, young or asymptomatic: observe; large, persistent or growing: endoscopic (internal) drainage
  • Fever, leukocytosis, gas or thick irregular wall: abscess or infected collection, percutaneous drainage
  • Septations, solid parts, no pancreatitis history: think cystic neoplasm
exam_pearl: Without a pancreatitis history and with septations or solid components, the same location points to a cystic neoplasm, not a pseudocyst.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 6 or 7 years old child fell and subsequently became drowsy, nauseated, and started vomiting. GCS is decreased but not ≤8 (I don't remember exactly) CT scan shows a crescent shaped intracranial bleeding. What is the best management?
why_right: After a fall, the child became drowsy, nauseated and vomiting with a reduced GCS, and CT shows a crescent-shaped bleed, which is a subdural hematoma (torn bridging veins). A symptomatic acute traumatic hematoma with neurological deterioration and raised intracranial pressure signs needs urgent neurosurgical evacuation to relieve mass effect. Because the GCS is not ≤8 and the airway is maintained, definitive decompression takes priority over intubation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Intubation is indicated for GCS ≤8, inability to protect the airway, hypoxia or aspiration risk; here the GCS is reduced but above 8, so the airway is not the immediate problem.
C. Reassurance fits a minor head injury with normal GCS and no imaging findings; a child with vomiting, drowsiness and an intracranial bleed on CT cannot be reassured.
D. CT already made the diagnosis and is the test of choice for acute head trauma; MRI only delays treatment and is reserved for subacute or subtle injuries (for example diffuse axonal injury).
key_concept:
Acute intracranial bleed on CT + deterioration = surgical evacuation.
  • Subdural: crescent (concave), bridging veins
  • Epidural: lens (biconvex), middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • CT without contrast is the first imaging in head trauma
  • Intubate if GCS ≤8 or airway not protected
  • Small, asymptomatic hematoma without shift: may be observed with serial CT
exam_pearl: If the stem gave GCS ≤8, airway first; with GCS above 8 and a symptomatic bleed, go to evacuation.

stem: A 23-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department after he fell down from 3 m height on his right leg. Examination revealed a deformity of the leg with an open wound in the mid-leg and devitalized tissue and dirt in the wound. The leg was put in a splint Blood pressure 112/70 mmhg Heart rate 99 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Oxygen saturation 95 % Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: devitalized tissue and dirt in the wound
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Surgical debridement (antibiotics-first is argued as the alternative).
  • Open fracture sequence: IV antibiotics + tetanus, splint or reduce
  • Then urgent debridement and irrigation in theatre
  • Then definitive fixation: IM nail, or external fixator if soft tissues are badly damaged
  • Lead-in decides: first step in ED = antibiotics; surgical next step = debridement
exam_pearl: If the stem says antibiotics were already given, debridement is unequivocally next.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: BP printed as '11270 mmhg' (likely 112/70).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A patient with diabetes presents with swelling of the big toe and warmth and tenderness of the calf for 4 days. There is a 2-cm ulcer over the first metatarsal area. No discharge is noted. Distal pulses are intact. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
highlight_terms_source: warmth and tenderness of the calf
why_right: The decisive clues are warmth and tenderness of the calf for 4 days with limb swelling and intact distal pulses: arterial insufficiency is unlikely and deep vein thrombosis (or venous disease) must be excluded. Duplex ultrasound is the non-invasive, first-line test that assesses venous flow and thrombus (and can also assess arterial flow), so it is the most appropriate initial investigation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Conventional angiography is invasive arterial imaging used for intervention planning in established arterial disease; with intact pulses it is not an initial test.
C. ABI is the first test for suspected peripheral arterial disease (claudication, absent pulses, arterial ulcer); it does not detect DVT and is often falsely high in diabetics with calcified vessels.
D. CT with contrast (or CT angiography) suits acute limb ischemia or deep abscess or osteomyelitis planning; it is not the initial test for a warm tender calf and carries contrast risk in a diabetic.
key_concept:
Leg problem: check the pulses first, then pick the test.
  • Pulses intact + calf swelling, warmth, tenderness: duplex ultrasound for DVT
  • Pulses intact + gaiter ulcer: venous duplex
  • Absent pulses, claudication: ABI first, then arterial duplex, then CT angiography
  • Acute ischemia (sudden pain, absent pulses): CT angiography
exam_pearl: A diabetic foot ulcer is a distractor here; the warm tender calf with intact pulses makes it a venous question.
